options.text: *Sōia ʻe faitala.*
options.explanation: The stop verb is right, but the general particle *te* is missing between the person and the verb.

questions.prompt: Can the two do-not verbs stand on their own, with no person and no verb after them? Which of these is right?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻAua.* means "Don't.", but *sōia* cannot stand alone and needs a person and a verb after it.
options.explanation: The first half is right, but *sōia* can also stand on its own, meaning "Stop.", when what to stop is clear.

options.label: B
options.text: *Sōia.* means "Stop.", but *ʻaua* cannot stand alone and needs a person and a verb after it.
options.explanation: The first half is right, but *ʻaua* can also stand on its own, meaning "Don't.", when what is forbidden is already plain.

options.label: C
options.text: Neither can stand alone; each needs a person and a verb after it.
options.explanation: Each of the two can stand on its own when the moment makes plain what is meant.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻAua.* means "Don't." and *Sōia.* means "Stop."
options.explanation: Correct: both can stand alone with no verb after them when what is forbidden or stopped is already clear.

questions.prompt: Read the English and choose the verb for the gap: *ʻAua tātou te ___.* (Let us not stay.)

options.label: A
options.text: *nonofo*
options.explanation: Correct: the group is more than one, so the verb for "stay" takes its plural form *nonofo*.

options.label: B
options.text: *nofo*
options.explanation: This is "stay", but in its singular shape, for one person; a group of more than one takes the plural.

options.label: C
options.text: *uli*
options.explanation: This is a plural form, but it means "black", not "stay".

options.label: D
options.text: *uliuli*
options.explanation: This means "black", not "stay", and it is the singular shape besides.

questions.prompt: This chapter has two notes, one on reporting that someone was told to stop and one on what can stand in place of *te* after *ʻaua*. Which of these states both correctly?

options.label: A
options.text: When you report that someone told another person to stop, *sōia* takes no particle at all; after *ʻaua* you will sometimes meet *neʻi* in place of *te*.
options.explanation: The second half is right, but in a reported command *sōia* takes the general particle *e*.

options.label: B
options.text: When you report that someone told another person to stop, *sōia* takes the general particle *e*; after *ʻaua* you will sometimes meet *neʻi* in place of *te*.
options.explanation: Correct: the reported pattern gives *sōia* the particle *e*, and *neʻi* is a word to recognize after *ʻaua*, from a family of mood words taught later.

options.label: C
options.text: When you report that someone told another person to stop, *sōia* takes the general particle *e*; after *ʻaua* you will sometimes meet *lē* in place of *te*.
options.explanation: The first half is right, but the word met after *ʻaua* in place of *te* is *neʻi*.

options.label: D
options.text: When you report that someone told another person to stop, *sōia* takes no particle at all; after *ʻaua* you will sometimes meet *lē* in place of *te*.
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: a reported *sōia* takes the particle *e*, and the word met after *ʻaua* in place of *te* is *neʻi*.

questions.prompt: The chapter's words *ola*, *meaola* and *tei*: what do they mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: life or live, then animals or living things, then little sister
options.explanation: Correct: *ola* is life or live, *meaola* is animals or living things, and *tei* is little sister.

options.label: B
options.text: go, then animals or living things, then little sister
options.explanation: The second and third are right, but *ola* is life or live; going is *alu*.

options.label: C
options.text: life or live, then food or things to eat, then little sister
options.explanation: The first and third are right, but *meaola* are animals or living things, not food.

options.label: D
options.text: life or live, then animals or living things, then friend
options.explanation: The first two are right, but *tei* is little sister; a friend is *uō*.

questions.prompt: What does *ʻAua ʻe te faʻasāunoa ʻi meaola* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop torturing animals.
options.explanation: The action is right, but this sentence opens with *ʻaua*, which forbids; stopping an action takes *sōia*.

options.label: B
options.text: Stop feeding animals.
options.explanation: This sentence forbids with *ʻaua* rather than stopping, and the verb *faʻasāunoa* is torture, not feed.

options.label: C
options.text: Do not torture animals.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻaua* forbids, *faʻasāunoa* is torture, and the thing reached, *meaola*, is pointed at with the place word *ʻi*.

options.label: D
options.text: Do not feed animals.
options.explanation: The forbidding is right, but the verb *faʻasāunoa* means torture or be cruel to, not feed.

questions.prompt: Each of these either denies a statement or forbids or stops an action. Which one is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: *Sā lē siva le tama.*
options.explanation: This is right: a statement has the tense particle *sā* for the not-word *lē* to follow, so it means "The boy did not dance".

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻAua ʻe te siva.*
options.explanation: This is right: the do-not verb forbids the action, "Don't dance".

options.label: C
options.text: *Sōia ʻe te tagi.*
options.explanation: This is right: the stop verb tells someone to stop an action under way, "Stop crying".

options.label: D
options.text: *Lē siva.*
options.explanation: Correct: this is the wrong one, because a command carries no tense particle for the not-word *lē* to follow; it is forbidden with the do-not verb instead.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the belonging words *a* and *o*?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *a* marks a relationship that is given, and *o* one the owner started and controls; the owner in an *a* phrase need not be a person; and the control rule sorts most words but not all.
options.explanation: The two jobs are the other way round: *a* marks what the owner started and controls, and *o* what is given.

options.label: B
options.text: The word *a* marks a relationship the owner started and controls, and *o* one that is given; the owner in an *a* phrase need not be a person; and the control rule sorts most words but not all.
options.explanation: Correct: control decides most words, an *a* owner is usually a person without having to be one, and the rest are learned word by word.

options.label: C
options.text: The word *a* marks a relationship the owner started and controls, and *o* one that is given; the owner in an *a* phrase must always be a person; and the control rule sorts most words but not all.
options.explanation: The owner in an *a* phrase is usually a person, because getting and using things is what people do, but it does not have to be one.

options.label: D
options.text: The word *a* marks a relationship the owner started and controls, and *o* one that is given; the owner in an *a* phrase need not be a person; and the control rule decides the belonging word of every word.
options.explanation: The control rule sorts most words, and some words sit where it does not put them, so their type is learned as a fact of the word.

questions.prompt: What do the chapter's words *atunuʻu*, *lanu*, *maʻamusa*, *paopao*, *pele* and *tao* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: colour, country, lover, canoe, darling, spear
options.explanation: The first two are the wrong way round: *atunuʻu* is "country" and *lanu* is "colour".

options.label: B
options.text: country, colour, darling, canoe, lover, spear
options.explanation: The two people-words are the wrong way round: *maʻamusa* is "lover" and *pele* is "darling".

options.label: C
options.text: country, colour, lover, spear, darling, canoe
options.explanation: The boat and the weapon are the wrong way round: *paopao* is "canoe" and *tao* is "spear".

options.label: D
options.text: country, colour, lover, canoe, darling, spear
options.explanation: Correct: all six meanings stand in the order of the words.

questions.prompt: How do you say "a house of mine" and "some cups of mine", in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: *soʻu fale*, *ni aʻu ipu*
options.explanation: Correct: one house of no particular identity takes *soʻu*, and more than one cup of no particular identity takes *ni* in front of *aʻu*.

options.label: B
options.text: *ni oʻu fale*, *ni aʻu ipu*
options.explanation: The first form names more than one house of no particular identity, "some houses of mine".

options.label: C
options.text: *soʻu fale*, *aʻu ipu*
options.explanation: The second form names more than one particular cup; "some" calls for *ni* in front.

options.label: D
options.text: *oʻu fale*, *ni aʻu ipu*
options.explanation: The first form names more than one particular house, not one house of no particular identity.

questions.prompt: Three of these are shown with their right meaning. Which one is not?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻo le sipuni a le fafine*, the spoon of the woman
options.explanation: This is right: *sipuni* is "spoon", and the woman is the owner.

options.label: B
options.text: *saʻu taʻavale*, a car of mine
options.explanation: This matches the chapter: *saʻu* is "a ... of mine", one thing of no particular identity.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻO loʻu ʻie.* My dress.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻie* is "kilt", so this says "My kilt".

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻO aʻu taʻavale.* My cars.
options.explanation: This matches: it is the chapter's own example for more than one particular car.

questions.prompt: Three of these are true of the belonging word each thing takes. Which one is not?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻofu* (dress) and *tao* (spear) both take *o*.
options.explanation: This is true: clothes worn and old tools and weapons are *o*-words, even though a dress is put on by choice.

options.label: B
options.text: *paopao* (canoe) and *igoa* (name) both take *o*.
options.explanation: This is true: boats and a name are *o*-words.

options.label: C
options.text: *fānau* (children) and *pele* (darling) both take *a*.
options.explanation: This is true: one's children and the people taken into a life are *a*-words.

options.label: D
options.text: *vaʻa* (boat) and *fana* (gun) both take *o*.
options.explanation: Correct: a boat takes *o*, but a gun is got and used, so it takes *a*.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the belonging words are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: *tamā* (father) and *pito* (end) both take *o*.
options.explanation: This is true: family by birth and a part of a whole are *o*-words.

options.label: B
options.text: *naifi* (knife) and *lanu* (colour) both take *a*.
options.explanation: Correct: a knife is got and used and takes *a*, but a colour is a quality of the thing itself and takes *o*.

options.label: C
options.text: *ulu* (head) and *atunuʻu* (country) both take *o*.
options.explanation: This is true: parts of the body and the place a person comes from are *o*-words.

options.label: D
options.text: A mother's son (*tama*) takes *a*, and a father's son takes *o*.
options.explanation: This is true: the same son is joined to his mother with *a* and to his father with *o*, and control does not explain it.

questions.prompt: Two words in this chapter differ only in their marks, *ʻava* and *āvā*. Which of these is true of them?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *ʻava* is "wife" and *āvā* is "beard"; the beard takes *a*, though parts of the body take *o*; and a wife takes *a*.
options.explanation: The meanings are the wrong way round: the word that begins with a catch in the voice is "beard", and the one with two long vowels is "wife".

options.label: B
options.text: The word *ʻava* is "beard" and *āvā* is "wife"; the beard takes *o*, like the other parts of the body; and a wife takes *a*.
options.explanation: The beard runs the other way from the rest of the body: it takes *a*.

options.label: C
options.text: The word *ʻava* is "beard" and *āvā* is "wife"; the beard takes *a*, though parts of the body take *o*; and a wife takes *a*.
options.explanation: Correct: the marks make two different words, and both take *a*, the beard against the body-part rule and a wife as a spouse.

options.label: D
options.text: The word *ʻava* is "beard" and *āvā* is "wife"; the beard takes *a*, though parts of the body take *o*; and a wife takes *o*, as family by birth does.
options.explanation: A spouse is an *a*-word, so a wife takes *a*.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the for-word *mo* and the with-word *ma*?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *mo* says who something is for, the aim of an action, or how long something lasts; *ma* also means "for" when a person is handed food to eat or a thing to keep; and the pair only partly echoes the *a* and *o* split.
options.explanation: Correct: the for-word covers the one who benefits, the aim and the length of time, the with-word covers food or a thing handed over, and the echo of *a* and *o* is a resemblance, not a rule.

options.label: B
options.text: The word *mo* says who something is for or the aim of an action, but never how long something lasts; *ma* also means "for" when a person is handed food to eat or a thing to keep; and the pair only partly echoes the *a* and *o* split.
options.explanation: The for-word also gives a length of time, as in "for a week".

options.label: C
options.text: The word *mo* says who something is for, the aim of an action, or how long something lasts; *ma* never means "for", and only takes a companion along or joins two doers; and the pair only partly echoes the *a* and *o* split.
options.explanation: The with-word also means "for" when a person is handed food to eat or a thing to keep.

options.label: D
options.text: The word *mo* says who something is for, the aim of an action, or how long something lasts; *ma* also means "for" when a person is handed food to eat or a thing to keep; and *ma* goes with the *a*-words and *mo* with the *o*-words, a rule to lean on.
options.explanation: The pair only looks that way in short forms of an older written Samoan, now very rare, so it is a resemblance and not a rule to lean on.

questions.prompt: What do *ʻO ʻupu a le tamāloa.* and *ʻO le lā ipu.* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: Some words of the man. Their cup (the two of them).
options.explanation: With no article, the first phrase names particular words, more than one; "some" would call for *ni*.

options.label: B
options.text: The words of the man. Their cup (the two of them).
options.explanation: Correct: the missing article marks more than one particular word, and the *le* in front of *lā* counts one cup.

options.label: C
options.text: The words of the man. Their cups (the two of them).
options.explanation: The *le* in front of the pronoun counts the things, so this is one cup; more than one would leave it out.

options.label: D
options.text: The word of the man. Their cup (the two of them).
options.explanation: One word would carry the article *le*; with none, the first phrase names more than one.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the forms *aʻu* and *oʻu*, and of the phrase *ʻO le lā ipu.*?

options.label: A
options.text: The form *aʻu* is "me" wherever it stands, even in front of a naming word; *oʻu* has its catch between its two vowels; and *ʻO le lā ipu.* has no *a* or *o* because with a pair of owners the belonging word is not required.
options.explanation: In front of a naming word the form is "my", as in *aʻu taʻavale*, "my cars"; only standing on its own is it "me".

options.label: B
options.text: In front of a naming word *aʻu* is "my", and on its own it is "me"; *oʻu* has its catch in the same place as the word for "I" met at the start of this book; and *ʻO le lā ipu.* has no *a* or *o* because with a pair of owners the belonging word is not required.
options.explanation: The catch in the possessive form falls between the two vowels; in the word for "I" it comes first.

options.label: C
options.text: In front of a naming word *aʻu* is "my", and on its own it is "me"; *oʻu* has its catch between its two vowels; and *ʻO le lā ipu.* has no *a* or *o* because *lā* and the belonging word have folded into one word, as in *laʻu*.
options.explanation: With a pair or a group of owners the pronoun stays a separate word, and the belonging word is simply not required.

options.label: D
options.text: In front of a naming word *aʻu* is "my", and on its own it is "me"; *oʻu* has its catch between its two vowels; and *ʻO le lā ipu.* has no *a* or *o* because with a pair of owners the belonging word is not required.
options.explanation: Correct: position decides between "my" and "me", the catch in *oʻu* sits between the vowels, and with a pair of owners the belonging word is not required.

questions.prompt: What is a spatial noun, and can the set of spatial nouns take new members?

options.label: A
options.text: A small word that works like an English preposition such as "behind", and the set takes new members freely.
options.explanation: Where English reaches for a preposition, Samoan uses a noun here, and the set is closed.

options.label: B
options.text: A noun that names a region of space belonging to a thing, such as its inside, its top or its back, and the set is closed: it takes no new members.
options.explanation: Correct: the spatial noun carries the meaning an English preposition would carry, and no new words join the set.

options.label: C
options.text: A noun that names a region of space belonging to a thing, such as its inside, its top or its back, and the set takes new members freely.
options.explanation: The first half is right, but the set is closed and takes no new members.

options.label: D
options.text: A small word that works like an English preposition such as "behind", and the set is closed: it takes no new members.
options.explanation: The set is closed, but a spatial noun is a noun that names a region, not a small word that works like a preposition.

questions.prompt: How do you say "The cat under the house" in Samoan?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻO le pusi ʻi lalo le fale.*
options.explanation: The belonging word *o* is missing before the house, so the frame has lost one of its four parts.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻO le pusi ʻi tua o le fale.*
options.explanation: The frame is whole, but its spatial noun is not the one for "under"; that word is *lalo*.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻO le pusi ʻi lalo o le fale.*
options.explanation: Correct: the place word *ʻi*, the spatial noun *lalo*, the belonging word *o*, then the house.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻO le pusi ʻi luma o le fale.*
options.explanation: The frame is whole, but its spatial noun is not the one for "under"; that word is *lalo*.

questions.prompt: Three rules govern how the spatial-noun frame is used. Which option states all three correctly?

options.label: A
options.text: The belonging word is always *o*; the frame can follow a verb, naming where the action happens or where the going is headed; and a direction noun can stand straight after *ʻi* with no belonging phrase.
options.explanation: Correct: a part of a whole takes *o*, the frame attaches to a verb as well as to a noun, and a direction noun can stand alone after *ʻi*.

options.label: B
options.text: The belonging word is *a*; the frame can follow a verb, naming where the action happens or where the going is headed; and a direction noun can stand straight after *ʻi* with no belonging phrase.
options.explanation: The belonging word is *o*, never *a*, because a thing's back or inside is part of it, given rather than got.

options.label: C
options.text: The belonging word is always *o*; the frame follows only a noun, never a verb; and a direction noun can stand straight after *ʻi* with no belonging phrase.
options.explanation: The frame also follows a verb, where it names the place the action happens or, after a verb of going, the place it is headed for.

options.label: D
options.text: The belonging word is always *o*; the frame can follow a verb, naming where the action happens or where the going is headed; but a direction noun after *ʻi* always needs a belonging phrase after it.
options.explanation: A direction noun can stand after the place word on its own, with no belonging phrase after it.

questions.prompt: What does *ʻUa ʻi luga le pusi.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: On top of the cat.
options.explanation: That would make the cat the thing measured against; here *luga* stands alone in the place slot of the where-sentence, and the cat is the one whose place it gives.

options.label: B
options.text: The cat is down.
options.explanation: The word for down is *lalo*; *luga* is up, on top.

options.label: C
options.text: Under the cat.
options.explanation: This reads *luga* as under and makes the cat the thing measured against, and both are wrong here.

options.label: D
options.text: The cat is up.
options.explanation: Correct: a bare spatial noun fills the place slot of the where-sentence, so this says where the cat is: up.

questions.prompt: In three of these options, both sentences say what the English beside them says. Which option has a sentence whose English is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻO le vaʻa ʻi tafatafa o le uafu.* The canoe beside the wharf; *ʻO le ʻato ʻi tala ane o le umu.* The basket alongside the oven.
options.explanation: Both match: *tafatafa* is beside, and *tala ane* is the space next to, alongside.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻO le ipu ʻi luga o le fala.* The cup on the mat; *ʻO le tusi ʻi fafo o le potu.* The book inside the room.
options.explanation: Correct: *fafo* is outside, so the second sentence says the book is outside the room; the first sentence matches.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻO le lāʻau ʻi tua o le fale.* The tree behind the house; *ʻO le nuʻu ʻi sisifo o le uafu.* The village west of the wharf.
options.explanation: Both match: *tua* is back, behind, and *sisifo* is West.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻO le taʻavale ʻi luma o le fale.* The car in front of the house; *ʻO le naifi ʻi totonu o le ʻato.* The knife inside the basket.
options.explanation: Both match: *luma* is front, and *totonu* is inside.

questions.prompt: Three of these options gloss both their words correctly. Which option has a wrong gloss?

options.label: A
options.text: *mātū* North, and *saute* South.
options.explanation: Both are right: *mātū* is North and *saute* is South.

options.label: B
options.text: *toga* South, and *sasaʻe* East.
options.explanation: Both are right: *toga* is the second word for South, and *sasaʻe* is East.

options.label: C
options.text: *gāgaʻe* eastward, a little to the east, and *gagaifo* westward, a little to the west.
options.explanation: Both are right: *gāgaʻe* reaches a little way east, and *gagaifo* a little way west.

options.label: D
options.text: *sisifo* West, and *gagafō* further towards the east.
options.explanation: Correct: *gagafō* is further towards the west, not the east; the gloss on *sisifo* is right.

questions.prompt: Which of these options has a wrong gloss? In the other three, both halves are right.

options.label: A
options.text: *gāgaʻe* eastward, a little to the east, and *tuāʻau* the space in front of the reef.
options.explanation: Correct: *tuāʻau* is the space behind the reef, not in front of it; the gloss on *gāgaʻe* is right.

options.label: B
options.text: *tai* the direction towards the sea, and *uta* the direction inland.
options.explanation: Both are right: *tai* points towards the sea, and *uta* points inland.

options.label: C
options.text: *gātai* seawards, a little towards the sea, and *gāʻuta* further inland, a little way inland.
options.explanation: Both are right: each reaches a little way along the line that *tai* and *uta* name.

options.label: D
options.text: *lumāfale* the front of the house, and *gagaifo* westward, a little to the west.
options.explanation: Both are right: *lumāfale* is one of the chapter's fused words, and *gagaifo* reaches a little way west.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the chapter's words are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Some spatial nouns also stand as ordinary nouns, so *totonu* can name the inside of a thing on its own.
options.explanation: True: these nouns are met most often in the frame, but not only there.

options.label: B
options.text: In *Na oso ʻi lalo le tama mai le solofanua.* no belonging phrase is needed after the spatial noun: the from-phrase at the end names the place instead.
options.explanation: True: *lalo* stands on its own here, and *mai le solofanua* names where the jump started.

options.label: C
options.text: Stretching the final vowel, as in *lugā*, brings the place nearer than the plain word does.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because the stretch adds emphasis and the stretched form reaches further off, so *lugā* is further up.

options.label: D
options.text: The sides named by *tala mai* and *tala atu* are reckoned from where the speaker stands, or from whoever else is in view.
options.explanation: True: the pair is measured from a person in the scene, not fixed on the thing itself.

questions.prompt: The chapter's words *tala mai* and *tala atu*: what do they mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: the side facing the speaker, and the side away from the speaker
options.explanation: Correct: *tala mai* is the near side, this side, and *tala atu* the far side, beyond.

options.label: B
options.text: the space next to, alongside, and the side away from the speaker
options.explanation: The second meaning is right, but alongside is *tala ane*; *tala mai* is the side facing the speaker.

options.label: C
options.text: the side facing the speaker, and the space next to, alongside
options.explanation: The first meaning is right, but alongside is *tala ane*; *tala atu* is the side away from the speaker.

options.label: D
options.text: the side away from the speaker, and the side facing the speaker
options.explanation: These are the right two meanings in the wrong order.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the fused word *tuāfale*?

options.label: A
options.text: It means the space beside the house; the belonging word and the article are gone, and the vowel at the join lengthens; and only *tua* and *luma* are recorded fusing this way.
options.explanation: The meaning is wrong: the word means the same as *tua o le fale*, the space behind the house.

options.label: B
options.text: It means the same as *tua o le fale*, the space behind the house; only the article is gone, and the vowel at the join stays short; and only *tua* and *luma* are recorded fusing this way.
options.explanation: The belonging word is gone as well as the article, and the vowel at the join lengthens.

options.label: C
options.text: It means the same as *tua o le fale*, the space behind the house; the belonging word and the article are gone, and the vowel at the join lengthens; and any spatial noun fuses this way, *totonu* included.
options.explanation: Only *tua* and *luma* are recorded fusing, so the fused words are learned as words, not made from the other spatial nouns.

options.label: D
options.text: It means the same as *tua o le fale*, the space behind the house; the belonging word and the article are gone, and the vowel at the join lengthens; and only *tua* and *luma* are recorded fusing this way.
options.explanation: Correct: *tua* joins straight onto *fale* with a long vowel at the join, and it and *luma* are the only spatial nouns recorded doing so.

questions.prompt: What do *māsina*, *mata*, *peʻa*, *susu* and *inu* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: eye, month, flying fox, milk, drink
options.explanation: This swaps the first two: *māsina* is month and *mata* is eye.

options.label: B
options.text: month, eye, milk, flying fox, drink
options.explanation: This swaps the third and fourth: *peʻa* is the flying fox and *susu* is milk.

options.label: C
options.text: month, eye, flying fox, milk, drink
options.explanation: Correct: *māsina* is month, *mata* is eye, *peʻa* is the flying fox, *susu* is milk and *inu* is drink.

options.label: D
options.text: month, eye, flying fox, drink, milk
options.explanation: This swaps the last two: *susu* is milk and *inu* is drink.

questions.prompt: What do *fafaga*, *sāisai*, *tatala*, *pusa* and *moa* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: feed, tie up, open, box, hen
options.explanation: Correct: *fafaga* is feed, *sāisai* is tie or tie up, *tatala* is open, *pusa* is box and *moa* is hen.

options.label: B
options.text: tie up, feed, open, box, hen
options.explanation: This swaps the first two: *fafaga* is feed and *sāisai* is tie up.

options.label: C
options.text: feed, open, tie up, box, hen
options.explanation: This swaps the second and third: *sāisai* is tie up and *tatala* is open.

options.label: D
options.text: feed, tie up, open, hen, box
options.explanation: This swaps the last two: *pusa* is box and *moa* is hen.

questions.prompt: The sentence *E tausi pepe e le fafine.* holds two words spelled *e*. What does each one do?

options.label: A
options.text: The first is the agent marker, and the second marks *le fafine* as the one cared for.
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: the first stands in front of the bare verb, and in this sentence the woman does the caring.

options.label: B
options.text: The first is the general particle in front of the bare verb, and the second is the agent marker, marking *le fafine* as the doer.
options.explanation: Correct: position tells them apart, with the general particle in front of a bare verb and the agent marker in front of a noun after the verb.

options.label: C
options.text: The first is the general particle in front of the bare verb, and the second marks *le fafine* as the one cared for.
options.explanation: The first half is right, but in this sentence the woman is the one doing the caring and the babies are the ones cared for.

options.label: D
options.text: The first is the agent marker, and the second is the agent marker too, marking *le fafine* as the doer.
options.explanation: The second half is right, but an *e* in front of a bare verb is the general particle, never the agent marker.

questions.prompt: What does *Sā sasa le teine e le tamāloa* say, and which phrase does it put forward as the new part?

options.label: A
options.text: The girl hit the man, and the girl is put forward as the new part.
options.explanation: The marker *e* stands on *le tamāloa*, so the man did the hitting, even though the girl is named first.

options.label: B
options.text: The man hit the girl, and the man is put forward as the new part.
options.explanation: The phrase put forward is the one standing right after the verb, and here that is *le teine*.

options.label: C
options.text: The girl hit the man, and the man is put forward as the new part.
options.explanation: Both halves are the wrong way round: the man carries the marker, and the girl stands right after the verb.

options.label: D
options.text: The man hit the girl, and the girl is put forward as the new part.
options.explanation: Correct: *e le tamāloa* names the doer wherever it stands, and *le teine*, right after the verb, is the part put forward.

questions.prompt: How do you say "The pig ate the taro" in Samoan?

options.label: A
options.text: *Sā ʻai e le puaʻa le talo.*
options.explanation: Correct: *e le puaʻa* names the pig as the doer, and *le talo*, the taro, stands bare after it.

options.label: B
options.text: *Sā ʻai e le puaʻa le popo.*
options.explanation: This says the pig ate the copra: *popo* is copra, and taro is *talo*.

options.label: C
options.text: *Sā ʻai le talo.*
options.explanation: This leaves the doer out, so it says only that the taro was eaten.

options.label: D
options.text: *Sā ʻai le popo.*
options.explanation: This names no doer and the wrong food: it says only that the copra was eaten.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of *Na fasi le gata.*, *Sā ʻai le teine ʻi le iʻa.* and *Sā ʻai le iʻa.*?

options.label: A
options.text: In the first the snake did the killing; in the second the girl ate part of the fish; the third can mean the fish ate or the fish was eaten, and the talk around it settles which.
options.explanation: The verb *fasi* names something done to somebody, so the bare *le gata* is the one killed, and nobody is named as the killer.

options.label: B
options.text: In the first the snake was killed; in the second the girl ate all of the fish; the third can mean the fish ate or the fish was eaten, and the talk around it settles which.
options.explanation: With the place word *ʻi*, the eating reached the fish without finishing it; eating all of it takes the agent marker on the girl.

options.label: C
options.text: In the first the snake was killed; in the second the girl ate part of the fish; the third can only mean the fish was eaten.
options.explanation: Both readings of the third are correct Samoan, and since the words give no clue which is meant, the context settles it.

options.label: D
options.text: In the first the snake was killed; in the second the girl ate part of the fish; the third can mean the fish ate or the fish was eaten, and the talk around it settles which.
options.explanation: Correct: the verb decides what the bare noun is, *ʻi* says the eating did not finish the fish, and only the talk around the third settles its reading.

questions.prompt: In *ʻUa sua le maʻumaga e puaʻa.*, who is doing the rooting, and which one does the verb *sua* answer to?

options.label: A
options.text: The pigs are doing it, and *sua* answers to the pigs.
options.explanation: The verb never counts the one carrying *e*, however many there are, so it counts the taro patch.

options.label: B
options.text: The taro patch is doing it, and *sua* answers to the taro patch.
options.explanation: The marker *e* stands on *puaʻa*, so the pigs are the doers and the taro patch is the one the rooting is done to.

options.label: C
options.text: The pigs are doing it, and *sua* answers to the taro patch.
options.explanation: Correct: *e puaʻa* marks the pigs as the doers, and the verb counts the unmarked *le maʻumaga*, which is why it is the singular form.

options.label: D
options.text: The taro patch is doing it, and *sua* answers to the pigs.
options.explanation: Both halves are reversed: the pigs carry *e* as the doers, and the verb counts the unmarked taro patch.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the doer of an action done to something else?

options.label: A
options.text: A doer pronoun in front of the verb, like *ia*, still needs *e*; when the doer is left out, nothing takes its place and the verb keeps its shape; in writing and in formal speech, a doer phrase after the verb always carries *e*.
options.explanation: A doer in the slot in front of the verb takes no marker at all: in *Sā ia sasa le tama* the doer *ia* is bare, and so is *le tama* after the verb.

options.label: B
options.text: A doer pronoun in front of the verb, like *ia*, takes no marker; when the doer is left out, nothing takes its place and the verb keeps its shape; in writing and in formal speech, a doer phrase after the verb always carries *e*.
options.explanation: Correct: the preverbal doer is unmarked, leaving the doer out adds nothing and changes nothing, and writing and formal speech always mark the doer phrase.

options.label: C
options.text: A doer pronoun in front of the verb, like *ia*, takes no marker; when the doer is left out, the verb changes to a passive shape; in writing and in formal speech, a doer phrase after the verb always carries *e*.
options.explanation: Samoan has no passive: the verb keeps the shape it already had, and dropping the doer phrase does the whole job.

options.label: D
options.text: A doer pronoun in front of the verb, like *ia*, takes no marker; when the doer is left out, nothing takes its place and the verb keeps its shape; in writing and in formal speech, a doer phrase after the verb often goes without *e*.
options.explanation: In writing and in formal speech the doer phrase always carries *e*; it is in other settings that it may go without it.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of leaving words out?

options.label: A
options.text: The doer goes freely, but the single participant of a sentence about a passing state of affairs never does; the one the action happens to goes only once it has been named before; where two clauses are joined, a place phrase is not simply dropped, and *ai* stands in for it.
options.explanation: The single participant of a sentence about a passing state of affairs goes as freely as the doer does.

options.label: B
options.text: The doer and the single participant of a sentence about a passing state of affairs both go freely; the one the action happens to goes as freely as they do; where two clauses are joined, a place phrase is not simply dropped, and *ai* stands in for it.
options.explanation: The one the action happens to is the part that has to be there, unless it has already been named in what came before.

options.label: C
options.text: The doer and the single participant of a sentence about a passing state of affairs both go freely; the one the action happens to goes only once it has been named before; where two clauses are joined, a place phrase is simply dropped, and nothing stands in for it.
options.explanation: Where two clauses are joined, a place phrase cannot simply be dropped; the pointing-back word *ai* stands in for it.

options.label: D
options.text: The doer and the single participant of a sentence about a passing state of affairs both go freely; the one the action happens to goes only once it has been named before; where two clauses are joined, a place phrase is not simply dropped, and *ai* stands in for it.
options.explanation: Correct: the three parts are not equal, and where two clauses are joined a place phrase cannot simply be dropped, so the pointing-back word *ai* stands in for it.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements are true of what this chapter teaches. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Where two clauses are joined, all three parts can go once the speaker judges their referents plain from the context.
options.explanation: This is true: where two clauses are joined, even the one the action happens to can go, once what it refers to is plain.

options.label: B
options.text: In intimate settings, both men and women use the agent marker at low frequency.
options.explanation: This is true: among intimates neither men nor women use it often.

options.label: C
options.text: Away from intimate settings, women use the agent marker a good deal more of the time than men do.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: away from intimate settings it is men who use it a good deal more of the time than women do.

options.label: D
options.text: The greater the social distance between speaker and audience, the more likely the marking is.
options.explanation: This is true: the more distance there is between speaker and audience, the more likely the marker is heard.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the maker-prefix *faʻa-*?

options.label: A
options.text: It marks the doer of the sentence, it is written together with the word after it as one word, and some words carrying it have drifted from the meaning of the word inside or rest on a piece that is no word on its own.
options.explanation: Marking the doer is the job of the agent marker *e*; the prefix builds a new word out of a noun or a verb.

options.label: B
options.text: It builds a new word out of a noun or a verb, it is written as a separate word in front of that word, and some words it builds have drifted from the meaning of the word inside or rest on a piece that is no word on its own.
options.explanation: The prefix and the word it is built on are written together as one word, never as two.

options.label: C
options.text: It builds a new word out of a noun or a verb, it is written together with that word as one word, and some words it builds have drifted from the meaning of the word inside or rest on a piece that is no word on its own.
options.explanation: Correct: taking the prefix off is where reading a built word starts, though a few built words have drifted and many are built on a piece that is no word on its own.

options.label: D
options.text: It builds a new word out of a noun or a verb, it is written together with that word as one word, and every word it builds keeps the meaning of the word inside, which always stands on its own.
options.explanation: Taking the prefix off is where reading starts, not always where it ends: a few built words have drifted, and many rest on a piece that is no word on its own.

questions.prompt: What do the words *tatalo*, *lotu* and *tulāfono* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: pray, religion, law
options.explanation: Correct: *tatalo* is pray, *lotu* is religion, and *tulāfono* is law.

options.label: B
options.text: stand, religion, law
options.explanation: The second and third meanings are right, but *tatalo* means pray.

options.label: C
options.text: pray, mountain, law
options.explanation: The first and third meanings are right, but *lotu* means religion.

options.label: D
options.text: pray, religion, salt
options.explanation: The first two meanings are right, but *tulāfono* means law.

questions.prompt: What does *Sā faʻagoto e le tama le vaʻa.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The boat sank.
options.explanation: That leaves out the one who made it happen: the built verb brings a doer into the sentence, and *e* marks the boy as that doer.

options.label: B
options.text: The boy made the boat sink.
options.explanation: Correct: *goto* is sink, the built word *faʻagoto* is make sink, and *e* marks the boy as the one who did it.

options.label: C
options.text: The boy made the boat go.
options.explanation: The doer is right, but the word inside the built verb is *goto*, sink, not the word for going.

options.label: D
options.text: The boat made the boy sink.
options.explanation: The agent marker *e* stands in front of *le tama*, so the boy is the doer and the boat is the one it was done to.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the words the prefix goes in front of are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: It goes in front of nearly any noun, but not in front of a spatial noun.
options.explanation: True: nearly any noun takes the prefix, and a spatial noun is the kind of noun that refuses it.

options.label: B
options.text: It goes in front of a verb that takes no doer of its own, but as a rule not in front of a verb that already takes one.
options.explanation: True: that is the ordinary rule, and the rule names one exception.

options.label: C
options.text: The verb *iloa* takes a doer of its own, and it refuses the prefix.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: *iloa* takes a doer of its own and takes the prefix anyway, the one exception the rule names.

options.label: D
options.text: Where a verb runs both with a doer and without one, the prefix appears to attach to the side that takes no doer.
options.explanation: True: on a verb that runs in both patterns, the prefix appears to attach to the side with no doer.

questions.prompt: The word *faʻalētatau* is built by a rule of this chapter on a word from its list. What does it mean?

options.label: A
options.text: In a fitting, proper fashion.
options.explanation: The not-word *lē* stands between the prefix and the base, so the built word denies the base rather than repeating it.

options.label: B
options.text: Uncertain, doubtful.
options.explanation: That meaning belongs to a word built on a different base; the word inside here is *tatau*, fit, proper.

options.label: C
options.text: To make something fit and proper.
options.explanation: The not-word *lē* in the middle makes this a negative, not a verb of making something happen.

options.label: D
options.text: In an unseemly fashion.
options.explanation: Correct: take the prefix off and what is left is *lē* and then *tatau*, fit, proper, so the built word denies it.

questions.prompt: Three of these words are paired with the meaning this chapter gives them. Which pairing is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: *aogā*: use, useful
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *aogā* means use, useful.

options.label: B
options.text: *mauga*: butter
options.explanation: Correct, this is the wrong pairing: *mauga* means mountain.

options.label: C
options.text: *iloa*: know, see, notice
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *iloa* means know, see, notice.

options.label: D
options.text: *tonu*: right, correct
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *tonu* means right, correct.

questions.prompt: How do you say "to salt" in Samoan?

options.label: A
options.text: *faʻapata*
options.explanation: This is built on *pata*, butter, so it means to butter.

options.label: B
options.text: *māsima*
options.explanation: The bare noun names the salt itself; the built word is what names the salting.

options.label: C
options.text: *faʻasuka*
options.explanation: This is the built word on another noun of the kitchen, not on the noun for salt.

options.label: D
options.text: *faʻamāsima*
options.explanation: Correct: *māsima* is salt, and on a noun of this kind the prefix builds a verb meaning to put what the noun names onto something.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of a negative built with the prefix?

options.label: A
options.text: It is gentler than denying with the not-word alone, *faʻalēaogā* takes a doer with *e* while *faʻalētonu* takes none, and the not-yet word *leʻi* sometimes stands in the middle in place of *lē*.
options.explanation: Correct: a bare quality word is bluntest, the not-word alone is gentler and the built word gentler still; the doer has to be learned with each word, and *leʻi* can stand where *lē* does.

options.label: B
options.text: It is blunter than denying with the not-word alone, *faʻalēaogā* takes a doer with *e* while *faʻalētonu* takes none, and the not-yet word *leʻi* sometimes stands in the middle in place of *lē*.
options.explanation: Wrapping the not-word inside a built word is the gentlest of the three ways, not a blunter one.

options.label: C
options.text: It is gentler than denying with the not-word alone, both *faʻalēaogā* and *faʻalētonu* take a doer with *e*, and the not-yet word *leʻi* sometimes stands in the middle in place of *lē*.
options.explanation: The two run in different patterns: *faʻalētonu* describes something and takes no doer.

options.label: D
options.text: It is gentler than denying with the not-word alone, *faʻalēaogā* takes a doer with *e* while *faʻalētonu* takes none, and only *lē* can ever stand in the middle.
options.explanation: The not-yet word *leʻi* sometimes stands in the middle in place of *lē*.

questions.prompt: Three of these are true of words built in the same sense as *faʻamauga*, and of the prefix on a whole phrase. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: A word built in this sense means having the qualities of, or being similar to, what stands behind the prefix.
options.explanation: True: in this sense the built word is a way of being, not a second thing of the same kind.

options.label: B
options.text: A word built in this sense takes no doer, and it usually stands beside another word to describe it.
options.explanation: True: it takes no doer at all and usually describes the word it stands beside.

options.label: C
options.text: Words built in this sense are characteristic of a literary and formal style.
options.explanation: True: this sense belongs to a literary and formal style.

options.label: D
options.text: When the prefix takes a whole phrase, article and all, the word it builds names things as often as it describes them.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: a construction built on a whole phrase is used only to describe something else, and it is seldom heard in the spoken language.

questions.prompt: Three of these sentences say what the English beside them says. Which one does not?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻUa tagi faʻatolu le tama.* The boy has cried three times.
options.explanation: In front of a number the prefix counts occasions rather than things, so the English matches.

options.label: B
options.text: *Sā faʻailoa e le teine le tala.* The girl knew the story.
options.explanation: Correct: the built word *faʻailoa* means show, make known, so this says "The girl made the story known".

options.label: C
options.text: *E leai se tagata e tū faʻamauga.* No man stands like a mountain.
options.explanation: The word *tū* is stand, and *faʻamauga* says how the standing is done, so the English matches.

options.label: D
options.text: *Sā faʻasuka e le teine le vai.* The girl sweetened the water.
options.explanation: The built word *faʻasuka* is built on *suka*, sugar, so the English matches.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the six direction words?

options.label: A
options.text: They stand in front of the verb; *mai*, *atu* and *ane* take their bearings from the speaker, and *aʻe*, *ifo* and *ʻese* from the event itself; and the point the speaker-based words measure from is usually the speaker but can be another person or thing the speaker picks out.
options.explanation: A direction word stands after the verb, in front of whoever did the action, never in front of the verb.

options.label: B
options.text: They stand after the verb, in front of whoever did the action; *mai*, *atu* and *ane* take their bearings from the speaker, and *aʻe*, *ifo* and *ʻese* from the event itself; and the point the speaker-based words measure from is always the speaker and never anyone else.
options.explanation: The point is usually the speaker, but the speaker can pick out another person or thing instead, most often the one a story is following.

options.label: C
options.text: They stand after the verb, in front of whoever did the action; *mai*, *atu* and *ane* take their bearings from the speaker, and *aʻe*, *ifo* and *ʻese* from the event itself; and the point the speaker-based words measure from is usually the speaker but can be another person or thing the speaker picks out.
options.explanation: Correct: all three parts are what the chapter teaches about where the words stand and what fixes their direction.

options.label: D
options.text: They stand after the verb, in front of whoever did the action; *aʻe*, *ifo* and *ʻese* take their bearings from the speaker, and *mai*, *atu* and *ane* from the event itself; and the point the speaker-based words measure from is usually the speaker but can be another person or thing the speaker picks out.
options.explanation: The two groups are the other way round: up is up and down is down whoever is speaking, so *aʻe*, *ifo* and *ʻese* are the ones fixed by the event.

questions.prompt: What does *Na alu ʻese le tama.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The boy went off, away from me and toward you.
options.explanation: That direction is measured from the speaker, and *ʻese* is measured from a point the event itself fixes.

options.label: B
options.text: The boy went past.
options.explanation: Going past is measured from where the speaker stands, and *ʻese* is measured from a point the event itself fixes.

options.label: C
options.text: The boy went down.
options.explanation: Down is the job of a different direction word; *ʻese* says away from a point.

options.label: D
options.text: The boy went away.
options.explanation: Correct: after a verb *ʻese* means away from a point, so the boy went away.

questions.prompt: How do you say "The boy went past" in Samoan?

options.label: A
options.text: *Na alu atu le tama.*
options.explanation: This sets a different direction word after the verb, not the one for going past.

options.label: B
options.text: *Na alu aʻe le tama.*
options.explanation: This says the boy went up.

options.label: C
options.text: *Na alu ane le tama.*
options.explanation: Correct: *ane* is along, passing the speaker by, so the boy went past.

options.label: D
options.text: *Na alu ifo le tama.*
options.explanation: This too sets a different direction word after the verb, not the one for going past.

questions.prompt: Three of these sentences are paired with the English this chapter gives them. Which pairing is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻOu te lē popole atu ʻia te ʻoe.* I do not worry about you.
options.explanation: The English matches: *popole* is worry, and the worry is turned toward the person spoken to.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻUa maua lou faʻamalu?* Have you got your handkerchief?
options.explanation: Correct: *faʻamalu* is umbrella, so the sentence asks whether you have got your umbrella.

options.label: C
options.text: *Na alu ifo le tama.* The boy went down.
options.explanation: The English matches: *ifo* is the direction word for down.

options.label: D
options.text: *Faʻatali atu.* Wait here until I come back. (Lit. "Wait, away from me.")
options.explanation: The pairing is right: the speaker is the one leaving, so the waiting is turned away from the speaker with *atu*; the two words say only that, as the literal line shows.

questions.prompt: What do the words *afi*, *leo*, *solosolo* and *tuagane* mean, in that order?

options.text: fire, voice, handkerchief, and brother (of a woman)
options.explanation: Correct: *afi* is fire, *leo* is voice, *solosolo* is handkerchief and *tuagane* is brother (of a woman).
