options.label: C
options.text: fire, voice, brother (of a woman), and handkerchief
options.explanation: The last two meanings are the right ones in the wrong order: *solosolo* is handkerchief and *tuagane* is brother (of a woman).

options.label: D
options.text: fire, house, handkerchief, and brother (of a woman)
options.explanation: House is *fale*, the word at the end of many of this chapter's sentences; *leo* is voice.

questions.prompt: Three of these words are paired with the meaning this chapter gives them. Which pairing is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: *ita*: angry, be angry
options.explanation: The pairing is right: *ita* is angry, be angry.

options.label: B
options.text: *osofaʻi*: wait
options.explanation: Correct: *osofaʻi* is attack, and wait is *faʻatali*.

options.label: C
options.text: *sasao*: blaze, burn fiercely
options.explanation: The pairing is right: *sasao* is blaze, burn fiercely.

options.label: D
options.text: *taʻoto*: lie (down)
options.explanation: The pairing is right: *taʻoto* is lie (down).

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about where words stand are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: A describing word and a direction word can both follow the verb, and the describing word comes first.
options.explanation: True: the describing word comes before the direction word.

options.label: B
options.text: Inside a spatial noun phrase, the direction word comes directly after the spatial noun, before the belonging word.
options.explanation: True: in *ʻi lalo ifo o le fale*, *ifo* stands directly after *lalo* and before *o*.

options.label: C
options.text: The direction word comes after the verb and in front of whoever did the action.
options.explanation: True: the verb comes first, then the direction word, then the doer.

options.label: D
options.text: The pointing-back word *ai* comes before the direction word.
options.explanation: Correct: this is false, because the direction word comes first and *ai* after it, as in *Sā nofo aʻe ai le tama.*

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about words linked to the direction words are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: The direction word *ʻese* is the word for "far" doing a second job.
options.explanation: Correct: this is false, because *ʻese* is the word for "different, strange" doing a second job.

options.label: B
options.text: The command word *ʻaumai* (bring) is an old verb of taking with *mai* fused onto its end.
options.explanation: True: *ʻaumai* carries *mai* inside it.

options.label: C
options.text: The compass noun for east carries *aʻe* inside it, and the one for west carries *ifo*.
options.explanation: True: *sasaʻe* (east) holds *aʻe* and *sisifo* (west) holds *ifo*, very likely from the rising and the setting of the sun.

options.label: D
options.text: The spatial nouns for this side and the far side are *tala* with a direction word after it.
options.explanation: True: they are *tala mai* and *tala atu*, *tala* (next to) with a direction word after it.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about *aʻe* and *ifo* are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Both are related to verbs of their own: *aʻe* go up, climb, and *ifo* bow down.
options.explanation: True: that is where their directions come from.

options.label: B
options.text: A word of this pair cannot be followed by *mai*, *atu* or *ane*.
options.explanation: Correct: this is false, because a word of this pair can be followed by *mai*, *atu* or *ane*, so one sentence can say both which way a thing went and whose way it was turned.

options.label: C
options.text: The word *aʻe* can carry a note of politeness.
options.explanation: True: it can, though it does not always.

options.label: D
options.text: The word *ifo* sometimes carries a note of humility.
options.explanation: True: it sometimes carries a note of humility or self-abasement.

questions.prompt: The sentences *Na sau le tama mai le fale.* and *ʻOloʻo taʻoto mai le teine ʻi le fale.* both carry *mai*. Which of these is true?

options.label: A
options.text: In the first *mai* is the from-word; in the second it is the direction word, turning the action toward the speaker; and a direction word is used whether or not anything moves.
options.explanation: Correct: a place noun directly after *mai* makes it the from-word, and with the doer after it *mai* is the direction word, here on a girl who is lying still.

options.label: B
options.text: In both *mai* is the direction word, turning the action toward the speaker; and a direction word is used whether or not anything moves.
options.explanation: In the first a place noun follows *mai* directly, and that makes it the from-word: the boy came from the house.

options.label: C
options.text: In the first *mai* is the from-word; in the second it is the direction word, turning the action away from the speaker, toward the person spoken to; and a direction word is used whether or not anything moves.
options.explanation: The direction word *mai* turns the action toward the speaker, not away.

options.label: D
options.text: In the first *mai* is the from-word; in the second it is the direction word, turning the action toward the speaker; and a direction word is used only where something moves.
options.explanation: A direction word needs no movement: the girl is not moving at all, and *mai* says she lies where the speaker is, or turned the speaker's way.

30.title: The Complement Clause: Can and Must

questions.prompt: What do *faitalia*, *lavā*, *ulaula*, *pologa* and *uso* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: be able; do as one pleases; smoke; slave; sibling (a man's brother, a woman's sister)
options.explanation: The first two meanings are the wrong way round: *faitalia* is doing as one pleases, and *lavā* is being able.

options.label: B
options.text: do as one pleases; be able; smoke; slave; sibling (a man's brother, a woman's sister)
options.explanation: Correct: *lavā* is mostly met as *lē lavā*, cannot, and *uso* is a man's brother or a woman's sister.

options.label: C
options.text: do as one pleases; be able; slave; smoke; sibling (a man's brother, a woman's sister)
options.explanation: The third and fourth meanings are the wrong way round: *ulaula* is to smoke, and *pologa* is a slave.

options.label: D
options.text: do as one pleases; be able; smoke; sibling (a man's brother, a woman's sister); slave
options.explanation: The last two meanings are the wrong way round: *pologa* is a slave, and *uso* is a sibling.

questions.prompt: In *ʻUa tatau ona ʻou alu*, which part is the complement clause, and what is it?

options.label: A
options.text: The clause *ʻou alu* after *ona*: it fills the slot a noun phrase would fill for what the sentence is about, and *ona* is the that-word that opens it.
options.explanation: Correct: the clause after *ona* is what the sentence is about, and the word in front of it says something about that clause.

options.label: B
options.text: The clause *ʻou alu* after *ona*: it fills the slot of the doer, the one a phrase marked with *e* fills, and *ona* is the that-word that opens it.
options.explanation: The complement clause fills the slot for what the sentence is about, not the slot of a doer marked with *e*.

options.label: C
options.text: The clause *ʻou alu* after *ona*: it fills the slot a noun phrase would fill for what the sentence is about, and *ona* is a tense particle, the one that clause carries.
options.explanation: The word *ona* is the that-word, the joining word that opens the clause; it is not a tense particle.

options.label: D
options.text: The half in front of *ona*, *ʻUa tatau*: it fills the slot of the doer, and *ona* is the that-word that closes it.
options.explanation: The complement clause is the clause after *ona*, which opens it; on its own, *ʻUa tatau* is unfinished.

questions.prompt: Both *Sā lē mafai ona ʻou alu* and *E sā ona inu* carry *sā*. Which job does it do in each, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: The word for "forbidden" in the first, and the past particle in the second.
options.explanation: Both are the wrong way round: nothing stands in front of the first *sā*, and the general particle *e* stands in front of the second.

options.label: B
options.text: The past particle in both.
options.explanation: The second *sā* has the general particle *e* in front of it, so it stands in the predicate slot as the word for "forbidden".

options.label: C
options.text: The past particle in the first, and the word for "forbidden" in the second.
options.explanation: Correct: nothing stands in front of the first *sā* and the slot after it holds *lē mafai*, while the general particle *e* stands in front of the second.

options.label: D
options.text: The word for "forbidden" in both.
options.explanation: Nothing stands in front of the first *sā*, and the slot after it holds *lē mafai*, so it is the past particle.

questions.prompt: Translate into English: *ʻUa taga ona inu ʻava mālosi.*

options.label: A
options.text: It is forbidden to drink alcohol.
options.explanation: Forbidden would be *sā*; *taga* means allowed, may.

options.label: B
options.text: It is allowed to drink milk.
options.explanation: The words *ʻava mālosi* mean alcohol, strong kava, not milk.

options.label: C
options.text: It is forbidden to drink milk.
options.explanation: Here both words are misread: *taga* means allowed, and *ʻava mālosi* is alcohol.

options.label: D
options.text: It is allowed to drink alcohol.
options.explanation: Correct: *taga* is allowed, may, and *ʻava mālosi*, strong kava, is alcohol.

questions.prompt: How do you say "The girl can come" in Samoan?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻUa tatau ona sau le teine.*
options.explanation: This says the girl must come; *tatau* is the obligation word, necessary, must.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻUa mafai ona sau le teine.*
options.explanation: Correct: *mafai* is can, able, and the girl who can come stands inside the clause after *ona*.

options.label: C
options.text: *E sā ona sau le teine.*
options.explanation: This says it is forbidden for the girl to come; *sā* here is the word for forbidden, must not.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻUa iloa e le tama ʻua sau le teine.*
options.explanation: This says the boy knows that the girl has come; nothing in it says what she can do.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of *mafai* and the not-word *lē*?

options.label: A
options.text: The person can be named on *mafai* as well as inside the clause after *ona*, or inside that clause alone; and *lē* in front of *mafai* says the thing could not be done.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻOu te lē mafai ona ʻou ʻai meaʻai* names the person on both sides, *Sā lē mafai ona ʻou alu* only inside the clause, and in both *lē* makes the whole ability negative.

options.label: B
options.text: The person has to be named on *mafai* as well as inside the clause after *ona*; and *lē* in front of *mafai* says the thing could not be done.
options.explanation: In *Sā lē mafai ona ʻou alu*, *mafai* carries no person, and the clause alone says who would have gone.

options.label: C
options.text: The person can be named on *mafai* as well as inside the clause after *ona*, or inside that clause alone; and *lē* in front of *mafai* says a thing that could be done did not happen.
options.explanation: Placed in front of *mafai*, *lē* makes the whole ability negative: the thing was not possible.

options.label: D
options.text: The person has to be named on *mafai* as well as inside the clause after *ona*; and *lē* in front of *mafai* says a thing that could be done did not happen.
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: the person may be named inside the clause alone, and *lē* in front of *mafai* says the thing was not possible.

questions.prompt: What do *faʻasā* and *faʻataga* mean, in that order, and how are they built?

options.label: A
options.text: allow, and forbid; each is a word of its own, not built from *sā* or *taga*.
options.explanation: The meanings are the wrong way round, and the two words are built from *sā* and *taga*.

options.label: B
options.text: forbid, and allow; each is a word of its own, not built from *sā* or *taga*.
options.explanation: The meanings are right, but these are the maker-prefix at work on *sā* and *taga*.

options.label: C
options.text: allow, and forbid; each is the maker-prefix at work on *sā* and on *taga*.
options.explanation: The build is right, but the meanings are the wrong way round: *faʻasā* is to make forbidden, which is to forbid.

options.label: D
options.text: forbid, and allow; each is the maker-prefix at work on *sā* and on *taga*.
options.explanation: Correct: *sā* is forbidden and *faʻasā* is to forbid, while *taga* is allowed and *faʻataga* is to allow.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the words that take a clause after *ona*, such as *mafai* and *tatau*, as this chapter sets them in sentences?

options.label: A
options.text: Set in a sentence, each stands bare, with no tense particle of its own in front of it; it and the clause after *ona* name one event, which the word grades; and that clause always follows it.
options.explanation: Every one of these words set in a sentence in this chapter has a tense particle in front of it, as *e* stands in front of *tatau* in *E tatau ona alu le tama*.

options.label: B
options.text: Set in a sentence, each has a tense particle of its own in front of it; it and the clause after *ona* name two separate happenings, one each; and that clause always follows it.
options.explanation: There is one event, named by the clause after *ona*, and the word in front grades it as possible, necessary, permitted or forbidden.

options.label: C
options.text: Set in a sentence, each has a tense particle of its own in front of it; it and the clause after *ona* name one event, which the word grades; and that clause always follows it.
options.explanation: Correct: in *E tatau ona alu le tama* the particle *e* stands in front of *tatau*, the going is the one event, and the clause comes after.

options.label: D
options.text: Set in a sentence, each has a tense particle of its own in front of it; it and the clause after *ona* name one event, which the word grades; and that clause may also be put in front of it.
options.explanation: The complement clause always follows the word that takes it, and nothing puts it in front.

questions.prompt: A complement clause can be joined to the word that takes it in two ways: set down with nothing between, or opened by *ona*. Which of these is true of the tense particles, in the sentences this chapter shows?

options.label: A
options.text: Set down with nothing between, the clause carries no tense particle; opened by *ona*, it carries none either, and sits under the tense of the word in front.
options.explanation: The clause set down with nothing between keeps a tense particle of its own, as *ʻua sau* does in *ʻUa iloa e le tama ʻua sau le teine*.

options.label: B
options.text: Set down with nothing between, the clause keeps a tense particle of its own, read against the time of the first half; opened by *ona*, it carries none, and sits under the tense of the word in front.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻUa iloa e le tama ʻua sau le teine* carries two tense particles, and *ʻUa mafai ona sau le teine* carries one.

options.label: C
options.text: Set down with nothing between, the clause keeps a tense particle of its own, read against the time of the first half; opened by *ona*, it keeps a tense particle of its own as well.
options.explanation: A clause opened by *ona* never carries a tense particle, as the bare *sau* in *ʻUa mafai ona sau le teine* shows.

options.label: D
options.text: Set down with nothing between, the clause carries no tense particle; opened by *ona*, it keeps a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: This is the wrong way round: the clause with nothing between keeps its own tense particle, and the clause after *ona* carries none.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about *tatau* are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *tatau* was met earlier as "fit, proper"; with a clause after *ona*, it is the obligation word, necessary, must.
options.explanation: This is true: the obligation reading comes with the clause after *ona*.

options.label: B
options.text: The construction names no one who is doing the requiring; the person who has to act appears inside the clause after *ona*.
options.explanation: This is true: in *E tatau ona alu le tama* the boy appears inside the clause, and no one is named as requiring it.

options.label: C
options.text: The sentence *E tatau ona alu le tama* says that the boy must go, and it cannot say that he should go.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: *tatau* covers what is fitting as well as what is required, so the same sentence covers "the boy should go".

options.label: D
options.text: In *ʻUa tatau ona ʻou alu* there is one event, the going, and *tatau* grades it as the necessary one.
options.explanation: This is true: nobody is doing one thing called being necessary and another called going.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the word *atu* set on a quality word?

options.label: A
options.text: It raises the quality to the top, the most of all, the quality word keeps its shape, and a sentence with it is complete without naming what it is compared with.
options.explanation: The word *atu* gives the comparative degree, stronger rather than strongest.

options.label: B
options.text: It carries the comparative degree, the quality word takes an ending as well to show the degree, and a sentence with it is complete without naming what it is compared with.
options.explanation: No ending is added: the quality word has the same shape with *atu* after it as without.

options.label: C
options.text: It carries the comparative degree, the quality word keeps its shape, and a sentence with it is complete without naming what it is compared with.
options.explanation: Correct: the degree arrives as a word standing after the quality word, and the other side of the comparison may be left unsaid.

options.label: D
options.text: It carries the comparative degree, the quality word keeps its shape, and a sentence with it must always go on to name what it is compared with.
options.explanation: A sentence built with *atu* is complete as it stands; naming the other side takes one more word.

questions.prompt: What do the words *aʻau*, *isu* and *ōfaga* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: reef, nose, nest
options.explanation: Correct: reef, nose and nest, as the Words to Learn list gives them.

options.label: B
options.text: wharf, nose, nest
options.explanation: The word *aʻau* is reef, not wharf.

options.label: C
options.text: reef, mouth, nest
options.explanation: The word *isu* is nose, not mouth.

options.label: D
options.text: reef, nose, egg
options.explanation: The word *ōfaga* is nest, not egg.

questions.prompt: Three of these words are paired with the meaning this chapter gives them. Which pairing is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: *moni*: true
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *moni* is true.

options.label: B
options.text: *finagalo*: wish
options.explanation: This pairing is right, and it is a polite word, never used of your own wish.

options.label: C
options.text: *saienitisi*: scientist
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *saienitisi* is scientist.

options.label: D
options.text: *faitotoʻa*: window
options.explanation: Correct, this is the wrong pairing: *faitotoʻa* is door.

questions.prompt: What does *E laʻitiiti atu le manulele i lo le maile.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The dog is smaller than the bird.
options.explanation: The word right after *atu* names what has more of the quality, and here that is the bird, while the dog stands in the phrase opened by *i lo*.

options.label: B
options.text: The bird is smaller than the dog.
options.explanation: Correct: the bird is what the sentence is about, and *i lo le maile* names the dog it is weighed against.

options.label: C
options.text: The bird is smaller than the cat.
options.explanation: The word *maile* is dog, and no cat is named in this sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: The fish is smaller than the dog.
options.explanation: The word *manulele* is bird, not fish.

questions.prompt: How do you say "The dog is the strongest"?

options.label: A
options.text: *E mālosi atu le maile.*
options.explanation: This says "The dog is stronger", a comparison with the other side left unsaid.

options.label: B
options.text: *E mālosi le maile.*
options.explanation: This says only "The dog is strong", with no word raising the degree at all.

options.label: C
options.text: *E sili ona mālosi le maile.*
options.explanation: Correct: *sili* means best or most, and with *ona* after it the dog's strength is raised to the top.

options.label: D
options.text: *E mālosi atu le maile i lo le manulele.*
options.explanation: This compares the dog with one other animal: "The dog is stronger than the bird".

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the than-word *i lo*?

options.label: A
options.text: The *lo* may be dropped, leaving the place word *ʻi* on its own, and the phrase it opens comes last in the sentence.
options.explanation: Correct: both forms are correct, this book prints the fuller *i lo* throughout, and its phrase comes after what the sentence is about.

options.label: B
options.text: The *lo* may be dropped, leaving the place word *ʻi* on its own, and the phrase it opens comes straight after the quality word, before what the sentence is about.
options.explanation: Dropping the *lo* is right, but the phrase comes last, after what the sentence is about.

options.label: C
options.text: Both words must always be said, and the phrase they open comes last in the sentence.
options.explanation: The *lo* can be dropped, and both forms are correct.

options.label: D
options.text: The *ʻi* may be dropped, leaving *lo* on its own, and the phrase it opens comes last in the sentence.
options.explanation: It is the *lo* that can be dropped; the place word *ʻi* stays.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of *sili*?

options.label: A
options.text: It takes *ona*, and the clause after *ona* carries a tense particle of its own; with *atu* and a phrase opened by *i lo* after it, it compares two named things.
options.explanation: The clause after *ona* carries no tense particle of its own.

options.label: B
options.text: It takes *ona*, and the clause after *ona* carries no tense particle of its own; it only ever raises a quality to the top, and never compares two named things.
options.explanation: With *atu* and an *i lo* phrase after it, *sili* compares two named things, as the dog and the bird are compared in this chapter.

options.label: C
options.text: It takes *ona*, and the clause after *ona* carries a tense particle of its own; it only ever raises a quality to the top, and never compares two named things.
options.explanation: Both halves miss: the clause after *ona* has no tense particle, and *sili* with *atu* and *i lo* compares two named things.

options.label: D
options.text: It takes *ona*, and the clause after *ona* carries no tense particle of its own; with *atu* and a phrase opened by *i lo* after it, it compares two named things.
options.explanation: Correct: the clause after *ona* takes no tense particle, and *sili* reaches a comparison when *atu* and *i lo* follow it.

questions.prompt: Which words fill the gap in *Sā siva le teine ___ le finagalo o le tamā.* so that it means "The girl danced in accordance with the father's wish"?

options.label: A
options.text: *e pei*
options.explanation: The gap wants a word of agreement, and *pei* does not claim agreement.

options.label: B
options.text: *e tusa ma*
options.explanation: Correct: *tusa* is equal, the same, in accordance with, and *ma* brings in the wish the dancing agrees with.

options.label: C
options.text: *e tusa*
options.explanation: The word *tusa* takes *ma* before what the first half agrees with, so the *ma* cannot be left out.

options.label: D
options.text: *i lo*
options.explanation: The than-word weighs one thing against another in a comparison of more and less, not of agreement.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about *pei* and *tusa* are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *pei* covers both "like" and "as if".
options.explanation: This is true: *pei* likens one thing to another, which is why one word covers both.

options.label: B
options.text: A *tusa* clause leaves out what the sentence is about, because the first half of the sentence has already named it.
options.explanation: This is true: Samoan leaves out what the first half has already named rather than say it twice.

options.label: C
options.text: What follows *pei* in this chapter is only ever a noun phrase opened by *o*, never a clause with a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: *pei* also takes a clause with a tense particle of its own, as when the boy spoke as if he had been there.

options.label: D
options.text: The *pei* clause hangs on the end of a finished sentence, with the general particle *e* in front of *pei*.
options.explanation: This is true: the clause follows a finished sentence and takes *e* in front of *pei*.

questions.prompt: What does *ʻO le ōfaga o le manulele ʻi luga o le koko.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The nest of the bird in the cocoa tree.
options.explanation: Correct: *koko* is cocoa, and the phrase places the nest on top of the cocoa.

options.label: B
options.text: The nest of the bird in the coconut tree.
options.explanation: The word *koko* is cocoa, not coconut.

options.label: C
options.text: The nest of the bird in the coffee tree.
options.explanation: The word *koko* is cocoa, not coffee.

options.label: D
options.text: The nest of the bird in the breadfruit tree.
options.explanation: The word *koko* is cocoa, not breadfruit.

questions.prompt: This book prints one verb as *fasi* and as *fasi=a*. What are the two shapes called, and how does ordinary Samoan writing print the second one?

options.label: A
options.text: *fasi* is the long form and *fasi=a* the short form; ordinary writing runs the two parts together with no mark.
options.explanation: The names are the other way round: the plain shape is the short form, and the one carrying an ending is the long form.

options.label: B
options.text: *fasi* is the short form and *fasi=a* the long form; ordinary writing prints the equals sign too.
options.explanation: The names are right, but the equals sign is this book's way of keeping the ending visible, and ordinary Samoan writing puts no mark there.

options.label: C
options.text: *fasi* is the short form and *fasi=a* the long form; ordinary writing runs the two parts together with no mark.
options.explanation: Correct: the long form is the short form plus an ending, and the equals sign is a learning aid of this book, not part of ordinary spelling.

options.label: D
options.text: *fasi* is the long form and *fasi=a* the short form; ordinary writing prints the equals sign too.
options.explanation: This is wrong on both counts: the ending makes the long form, and ordinary writing puts no mark between the two parts.

questions.prompt: What do the words *tōtōga* and *vāega* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: internal organs, and section or part
options.explanation: Correct: *tōtōga* means internal organs, and *vāega* means a section or part.

options.label: B
options.text: section or part, and internal organs
options.explanation: These are the right two meanings in the wrong order.

options.label: C
options.text: internal organs, and cloth
options.explanation: The first meaning is right, but *vāega* means a section or part, not cloth.

options.label: D
options.text: window, and section or part
options.explanation: The second meaning is right, but *tōtōga* means internal organs, not a window.

questions.prompt: The chapter's forbidding sentence *ʻAua le ___ le vaʻa lenā.* means "Don't sell that boat." Which form fills the gap?

options.label: A
options.text: *faʻatau*
options.explanation: This is the short form, and a forbidding sentence built with *ʻaua le* takes the long form; speakers reject the short form there.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻaia*
options.explanation: This is a long form, but of *ʻai*, eat, not of the verb for selling.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻai*
options.explanation: This is the short form of *ʻai*, eat, so it is wrong on both counts.

options.label: D
options.text: *faʻatau=a*
options.explanation: Correct: after *ʻaua le* the verb takes its long form, and *faʻatau* is the trading verb, sell or buy. The *=ina* ending would be equally correct here.

questions.prompt: The chapter's command *___.* means "Read." Which form fills the gap?

options.label: A
options.text: *faitau=a*
options.explanation: This is a long form, and the long form never appears in a command to do something.

options.label: B
options.text: *faitau*
options.explanation: Correct: a command to do something takes the short form, and *faitau* means count or read.

options.label: C
options.text: *fau=a*
options.explanation: This is the long form of *fau*, build, so it is wrong on both counts.

options.label: D
options.text: *fau*
options.explanation: This is the short form, as a command needs, but *fau* means build, so the command would be "Build."

questions.prompt: What does *Sā nonoa le ʻie ʻi le faʻamalama.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The cloth was hung at the window.
options.explanation: The verb *nonoa* means tie up, not hang.

options.label: B
options.text: The rope was tied at the window.
options.explanation: The word *ʻie* means cloth, not rope.

options.label: C
options.text: The cloth was tied at the window.
options.explanation: Correct: *nonoa* is tie up, *ʻie* is cloth, and *faʻamalama* is window.

options.label: D
options.text: The cloth was tied at the fence.
options.explanation: The word *faʻamalama* means window, not fence.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: The ending *=ia* is a long-form ending that some speakers use, usually with a consonant in front of it.
options.explanation: This is true: *=ia* is a third long-form ending that some speakers use, usually with a consonant in front of it.

options.label: B
options.text: Which of *=a* and *=ina* a verb takes is settled by the verb alone, and the occasion plays no part.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: which ending a verb takes is partly a matter of the verb and partly of the occasion.

options.label: C
options.text: The ending *=na* is uncommon: recognise it, and build your own long forms with *=a* or *=ina*.
options.explanation: This is true: *=na* is on record but uncommon, so you recognise it and build with the two ordinary endings.

options.label: D
options.text: In *ʻAua ʻe te faitala* ("Don't gossip"), the verb rightly keeps its one shape even though the sentence forbids.
options.explanation: This is true: *faitala* takes no agent marker, and a verb of that kind has only one shape to offer.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true about which verbs have both a short and a long form?

options.label: A
options.text: A verb that runs both with the agent marker and without it has both shapes in the uses where the marker appears. A verb made agent-taking by an ending in the first place is regularly given a long form, heard as often as the long form of other verbs.
options.explanation: The first half is right, but such a derived verb is often used with one shape doing the work of both, and speakers who give it a long form use it less often than the long form of other verbs.

options.label: B
options.text: A verb that runs both with the agent marker and without it has both shapes in the uses without the marker, and a single shape where the marker appears. A verb made agent-taking by an ending in the first place is often used with one shape doing the work of both.
options.explanation: The second half is right, but a verb that runs in both patterns has both shapes in its uses with the agent marker.

options.label: C
options.text: A verb that runs both with the agent marker and without it has both shapes in the uses without the marker, and a single shape where the marker appears. A verb made agent-taking by an ending in the first place is regularly given a long form, heard as often as the long form of other verbs.
options.explanation: This is wrong on both counts: the two shapes go with the uses that take the agent marker, and a derived verb often lets one shape do both jobs.

options.label: D
options.text: A verb that runs both with the agent marker and without it has both shapes in the uses where the marker appears. A verb made agent-taking by an ending in the first place is often used with one shape doing the work of both.
options.explanation: Correct: the two shapes go with the uses that take the agent marker, and a verb already made agent-taking by an ending often lets one shape do both jobs.

questions.prompt: Where a verb can take either *=a* or *=ina*, which of these is true?

options.label: A
options.text: The ending *=a* is preferred in casual speech and *=ina* in formal speaking and writing, and formal writing also runs to forms built from two endings at once.
options.explanation: Correct: *=a* is the everyday choice and *=ina* the formal one, and forms with two endings at once are much rarer in casual speech.

options.label: B
options.text: The ending *=ina* is preferred in casual speech and *=a* in formal speaking and writing, and formal writing also runs to forms built from two endings at once.
options.explanation: The split runs the other way: *=a* is the everyday choice, and *=ina* is preferred in formal speaking and writing.

options.label: C
options.text: The ending *=a* is preferred in casual speech and *=ina* in formal speaking and writing, and no form is ever built from two endings at once.
options.explanation: The split is right, but formal writing does run to forms built from two endings at once.

options.label: D
options.text: The ending *=ina* is preferred in casual speech and *=a* in formal speaking and writing, and no form is ever built from two endings at once.
options.explanation: This is wrong on both counts: *=a* is the everyday choice, and formal writing does run to forms with two endings.

questions.prompt: Outside commands and forbidding sentences, which of these is true?

options.label: A
options.text: A fixed rule settles the shape, with the long form as the default. The long form is heard where the doer matters. A question asking who did it marks the question word with *ʻo*, not with the agent marker *e*.
options.explanation: The last two are right, but here the choice is open, and the short form is the default.

options.label: B
options.text: The choice is open, with the short form as the default. The long form is heard where the attention is on the thing acted on. A question asking who did it marks the question word with *ʻo*, not with the agent marker *e*.
options.explanation: The tendency runs the other way: the short form goes with attention on the thing acted on, and the long form with a doer who matters.

options.label: C
options.text: The choice is open, with the short form as the default. The long form is heard where the doer matters. A question asking who did it marks the question word with the agent marker *e*, as it would a named doer.
options.explanation: A doer asked for with the question word takes *ʻo ai* and no agent marker *e*.

options.label: D
options.text: The choice is open, with the short form as the default. The long form is heard where the doer matters. A question asking who did it marks the question word with *ʻo*, not with the agent marker *e*.
options.explanation: Correct: past the two command rules the choice is a tendency and not a rule, and the question word for a doer carries *ʻo* in place of *e*.

questions.prompt: In *ʻO ai na faʻatau mai=a le tusi?*, which of these is true?

options.label: A
options.text: It asks who sold the book, and it means the same as *ʻO ai na faʻatau=a mai le tusi?*
options.explanation: With *mai* the trade runs toward here, so this is buying; selling takes *atu*.

options.label: B
options.text: It asks who bought the book, and it means the same as *ʻO ai na faʻatau=a mai le tusi?*
options.explanation: Correct: *mai* makes the trading verb mean buying, and the ending may sit on the verb or move onto the direction word with no change of meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: It asks who sold the book, and its ending is out of place, since the ending can only sit on the verb.
options.explanation: This is wrong on both counts: *mai* makes it buying, and the ending may move onto a direction word that follows the verb.

options.label: D
options.text: It asks who bought the book, but its ending is out of place, since the ending can only sit on the verb.
options.explanation: The meaning is right, but when a direction word follows the verb, the ending can move onto it.

questions.prompt: When Samoan reports what somebody knew, how is the report built?

options.label: A
options.text: It is joined to the knowing half by a linking word, and it keeps a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: The tense particle is right, but for a report of what somebody knew nothing joins the report to the knowing half.

options.label: B
options.text: It follows the knowing word with nothing joining the two, and it keeps a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: Correct: the report is an ordinary clause set down after the knowing word, and it carries a tense particle of its own.

options.label: C
options.text: It follows the knowing word with nothing joining the two, and it has no tense particle of its own, the first half's particle covering both.
options.explanation: Nothing joins the two, but the report keeps a tense particle of its own; the first half's particle does not cover it.

options.label: D
options.text: It is joined to the knowing half by a linking word, and it has no tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: Wrong twice: nothing joins the two halves, and the report keeps a tense particle of its own.

questions.prompt: The words *ʻavatu*, *fusi* and *vaʻalele* are new in this chapter. What do they mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: order, belt, airplane
options.explanation: Order or instruct is *faʻatonu*; *ʻavatu* is give, away from the speaker.

options.label: B
options.text: give (away from the speaker), cloth, airplane
options.explanation: Cloth is *ʻie*, met earlier in this book; *fusi* is belt.

options.label: C
options.text: give (away from the speaker), belt, airplane
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻavatu* is give, away from the speaker, *fusi* is belt, and *vaʻalele* is airplane.

options.label: D
options.text: give (away from the speaker), belt, boat
options.explanation: The word *vaʻalele* is airplane, not boat.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the say-verb *fai*, in the pattern this chapter teaches, are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: What was said may be quoted word for word, or passed on in the reporter's own words.
options.explanation: This is true: the pattern takes a direct quotation or a report in your own words.

options.label: B
options.text: What was said comes after the say-verb, and it may run to more than one sentence.
options.explanation: This is true: what was said is a whole sentence of its own after the verb, and it may run longer than one.

options.label: C
options.text: The say-verb appears with either direction word, *atu* for speech going away from the speaker and *mai* for speech coming toward.
options.explanation: This is true: both *fai atu* and *fai mai* are used.

options.label: D
options.text: The noun phrase straight after *fai* names what was said.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: in this pattern the noun phrase after *fai* names the speaker, and what was said follows it as a sentence of its own.

questions.prompt: What does *Na iloa e le tama ʻoloʻo nofo le teine ʻi le nuʻu.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The boy knew that the girl had stayed in the village.
options.explanation: Here *ʻoloʻo* puts the staying at the same time as the knowing, not before it.

options.label: B
options.text: The boy knew that the girl is staying in the village.
options.explanation: That reads *ʻoloʻo* against the moment of speaking; here the staying is placed at the time of the knowing, which is past, so it was going on then.

options.label: C
options.text: The boy knew that the girl was staying in the village.
options.explanation: Correct: the knowing is past, and *ʻoloʻo* puts the staying at the same time as the knowing.

options.label: D
options.text: The boy knew that the girl has stayed in the village.
options.explanation: Wrong twice: *ʻoloʻo* marks the staying as going on, not done, and it places it at the time of the knowing, not now.

questions.prompt: What does *Na iloa e loʻu ataliʻi ʻua sasae le ʻie.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: My son knew that the cloth had been torn.
options.explanation: Correct: *ataliʻi* is son, *sasae* is tear, and *ʻua* marks the tearing as already done by the time of the knowing.

options.label: B
options.text: My son knew that the cloth would be torn.
options.explanation: Here *ʻua* marks the tearing as already done by the time of the knowing, not still to come.

options.label: C
options.text: My son knew that the cloth had been fastened.
options.explanation: The verb *sasae* is tear, not fasten.

options.label: D
options.text: My daughter knew that the cloth had been torn.
options.explanation: The word *ataliʻi* is son.

questions.prompt: How do you say "The boy knows that the girl had stayed in the village"?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻUa iloa e le tama ʻoloʻo nofo le teine ʻi le nuʻu.*
options.explanation: This one says the girl is staying, at the same time as the knowing.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻUa iloa e le tama sā nofo le teine ʻi le nuʻu.*
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻUa iloa* sets the report at now, and *sā* puts the staying before it.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻUa iloa e le tama e nofo le teine ʻi le nuʻu.*
options.explanation: The general particle *e* in the reported half does not put the staying before the knowing, so this one does not say "had stayed".

options.label: D
options.text: *Na iloa e le tama sā nofo le teine ʻi le nuʻu.*
options.explanation: The reported half is right, but *Na iloa* sets the report in the past: "The boy knew that the girl had stayed in the village".

questions.prompt: In a reported clause, what do *ʻoleʻā* and the general particle *e* each do to the time of the reported event?

options.label: A
options.text: The particle *ʻoleʻā* puts it after the moment of speaking, and *e* puts it at the same time as the report.
options.explanation: Wrong twice: *ʻoleʻā* is read against the time of the report, not the moment of speaking, and *e* sets no time of its own.

options.label: B
options.text: The particle *ʻoleʻā* puts it after the time of the report, and *e* puts it at the same time as the report.
options.explanation: Right about *ʻoleʻā*, but *e* sets no time of its own; *ʻoloʻo* is the particle that puts an event at the same time as the report.

options.label: C
options.text: The particle *ʻoleʻā* puts it after the moment of speaking, whatever time the report names, and *e* sets no time of its own.
options.explanation: Right about *e*, but *ʻoleʻā* is read against the time of the report, so under a past report it gives "would come", not a coming still ahead of now.

options.label: D
options.text: The particle *ʻoleʻā* puts it after the time of the report, and *e* sets no time of its own.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻoleʻā* marks an event still to come at the time of the report, and *e* sets no time of its own.

questions.prompt: Which word fills the gap in *Na fai mai le teine ___ alu le tama.* so that it means "The girl asked whether the boy would go"?

options.label: A
options.text: *pē*
options.explanation: Correct: when what is reported is a question, the reported sentence opens with *pē*.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻoleʻā*
options.explanation: A tense particle does not open a reported question, even one about something still to come.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻia*
options.explanation: The mood particle *ʻia* opens a reported command, not a reported question.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻua*
options.explanation: A tense particle does not open a reported question, and *ʻua* would mark the going as already done.

questions.prompt: The new word *tā* is spelled like the word for "you and I" taught earlier in this book. What tells the two apart, and what does the new *tā* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Position: the new *tā* stands between the tense particle and the verb or inside a possessive phrase, while the pronoun stands where the verb stands; it means beat, strike or play.
options.explanation: Right meaning, but the positions are reversed: the new *tā* is the verb itself, and the pronoun stands between the tense particle and the verb or inside a possessive phrase.

options.label: B
options.text: Position: the new *tā* stands where the verb stands, while the pronoun stands between the tense particle and the verb or inside a possessive phrase; it means beat, strike or play.
options.explanation: Correct: position tells them apart, and the verb *tā* means beat, strike or play.

options.label: C
options.text: Position: the new *tā* stands where the verb stands, while the pronoun stands between the tense particle and the verb or inside a possessive phrase; it means tear.
options.explanation: Right on position, but tear is *sasae*; the new *tā* is beat, strike or play.

options.label: D
options.text: Position: the new *tā* stands between the tense particle and the verb or inside a possessive phrase, while the pronoun stands where the verb stands; it means tear.
options.explanation: Wrong twice: the positions are reversed, and tear is *sasae*.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about reported commands and reported questions are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: A reported command opens with *ʻia*, which stands where a tense particle would otherwise stand.
options.explanation: This is true: *ʻia* fills the first slot of the reported clause, and what follows it is what somebody is to do.

options.label: B
options.text: In a reported command the general particle *e* can stand in place of *ʻia*, with the same reading.
options.explanation: This is true: *e* also stands in that slot, with the same reported-command reading.

options.label: C
options.text: A reported question can open with *po*, the other shape of *pē*.
options.explanation: This is true: *po*, the question marker met earlier in this book, is the other shape of *pē*, and either shape opens a reported question.

options.label: D
options.text: With *faʻatonu*, the one who gives the order stands after the verb with no marker.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: the one who gives the order takes the agent marker *e*, as *e le tama* does after *faʻatonu mai*.

questions.prompt: How do you say "only" and "any" in Samoan, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: *soʻo se* and *naʻo*
options.explanation: These are the right two words in the wrong order.

options.label: B
options.text: *naʻo* and *lea*
options.explanation: The first is right, but the word for "any" is *soʻo se*, not *lea*.

options.label: C
options.text: *naʻo* and *soʻo se*
options.explanation: Correct: *naʻo* is "only" and *soʻo se* is "any".

options.label: D
options.text: *ai* and *soʻo se*
options.explanation: The second is right, but the word for "only" is *naʻo*, and *ai* is the pointing-back word.

questions.prompt: What do the words *tapē* and *ʻuma* mean, in that order?

options.label: B

options.label: C

options.explanation: The second is right, but *tapē* means kill, not open.

options.label: D
options.text: kill; work

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about putting a phrase at the head of a sentence are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: At the head of a sentence, the presenting particle *ʻo* lifts a noun phrase out of its ordinary slot and holds it up.
options.explanation: True: this is the particle's job at the head of a sentence.

options.label: B
options.text: The whole phrase goes to the head together, however many words it runs to.
options.explanation: True: in the chapter's sentence about the voice of the baby, all five words of that phrase travel to the front together.

options.label: C
options.text: Samoan writers usually print *naʻo* as two words, *na o*, though this book prints it as one.
options.explanation: True: the two-word spelling is the usual one in Samoan writing, and this book keeps to one word.

options.label: D
options.text: A phrase headed by *naʻo* or *soʻo se* takes *ʻo* in front of it when it goes to the head of a sentence.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because a phrase headed by either word goes to the head bare, with neither *ʻo* nor *ʻi* in front of it.

questions.prompt: What does *Soʻo se tagata e tatau ona ʻaumai se falaoa.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Anybody should bring some bread.
options.explanation: Correct: the phrase at the head means "any person", and *falaoa* is bread.

options.label: B
options.text: Only the person should bring some bread.
options.explanation: The word for "only" is *naʻo*, and this sentence opens on the word for "any".

options.label: C
options.text: Anybody should bring some fish.
options.explanation: The word *falaoa* is bread, not fish.

options.label: D
options.text: Anybody should bring some water.
options.explanation: The word *falaoa* is bread, not water.

questions.prompt: Three of these words are paired with the meaning this chapter gives them. Which pairing is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: *lagona*: hear, feel
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *lagona* means hear, feel.

options.label: B
options.text: *leaga*: bad
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *leaga* means bad.

options.label: C
options.text: *faʻatoʻaga*: door
options.explanation: Correct: *faʻatoʻaga* is plantation, and the word for door is *faitotoʻa*.

options.label: D
options.text: *faleoʻo*: a small house
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *faleoʻo* means a small house.

questions.prompt: The sentence *Sā tapē e le tama le puaʻa.* can be said with either participant put first. Which is true of the shape of the verb when you do?

options.label: A
options.text: With either participant first it usually takes the long form *tapē=ina*, and this is a tendency rather than a rule.
options.explanation: Only a doer at the front leans toward the long form; a thing acted on at the front mostly keeps the short form *tapē*.

options.label: B
options.text: With the thing acted on first it mostly keeps the short form *tapē*, with the doer first it usually takes the long form *tapē=ina*, and both are tendencies rather than rules.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻO le puaʻa sā tapē e le tama* keeps the short form and *ʻO le tama sā tapē=ina le puaʻa* takes the long one, though usage varies from speaker to speaker.

options.label: C
options.text: With either participant first it mostly keeps the short form *tapē*, and this is a tendency rather than a rule.
options.explanation: Only a thing acted on at the front leans toward the short form; a doer at the front usually takes the long form *tapē=ina*.

options.label: D
options.text: With the thing acted on first it always keeps the short form *tapē*, with the doer first it always takes the long form *tapē=ina*, and neither choice has exceptions.
options.explanation: Both leanings are tendencies that vary by speaker and by verb, and the two command rules are the only exceptionless ones.

questions.prompt: The words *lea* and *ia* can point back to a phrase put first. Which of these is true?

options.label: A
options.text: They point back to a thing acted on put first, *lea* for one thing and *ia* for more than one, and a doer put first is never said a second time later in the sentence.
options.explanation: A doer put first can be said again by a middle-slot pronoun, as *aʻu* is by *ʻou*, though it need not be.

options.label: B
options.text: They point back to a thing acted on put first, *ia* for one thing and *lea* for more than one, and a doer put first can be said again by a middle-slot pronoun.
options.explanation: The number runs the other way: *lea* points back to one thing and *ia* to more than one.

options.label: C
options.text: They point back to a doer put first, *lea* for one and *ia* for more than one, while a thing acted on put first can be said again by a middle-slot pronoun.
options.explanation: A thing acted on put first is never answered by a middle-slot pronoun, and it is the one *lea* and *ia* point back to.

options.label: D
options.text: They point back to a thing acted on put first, *lea* for one thing and *ia* for more than one, and a doer put first can be said again by a middle-slot pronoun.
options.explanation: Correct: in *ʻO aʻu ʻou te nofo ʻi totonu o le fale* the doer is said twice, while a thing acted on can be pointed back to by *lea* or *ia* after the verb.

questions.prompt: Putting a phrase first does four jobs. Three of these statements about them are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Weight on one word: moving a phrase to the front marks it as the point of the sentence only when a word of emphasis is added as well.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because the move alone does it, as in *ʻO le tama sā tapē=ina le puaʻa*, where nothing else differs from the ordinary order.

options.label: B
options.text: Naming the topic: a phrase put first announces what the rest is going to be about, which is why Samoan stories so often open this way.
options.explanation: True: this is the first job, and it is why a story so often opens with a phrase put first.

options.label: C
options.text: Contrast: two sentences set side by side, each with its person at the front, set the two people against each other.
options.explanation: True: *ʻO aʻu na ʻou vaʻai ʻi ai* beside *ʻO ʻoe ʻe te leʻi vaʻai ʻi ai* sets the speaker against the listener.

options.label: D
options.text: The setting: a phrase saying where or when something happened can be put first to give the where and when of the sentence.
options.explanation: True: this is the job the place phrases put first are doing.

questions.prompt: Which is true of the pointing-back word *ai* when a setting goes to the head of a sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: It stands straight after the setting, before the verb; with the place word *ʻi* kept it is normal but can be left out; and with the setting presented by *ʻo* it appears as well.
options.explanation: The pointing-back word answers the setting from inside the verb phrase, after the verb, as in *ʻi le faʻatoʻaga sā galue ai le tama*.

options.label: B
options.text: It stands after the verb; with the place word *ʻi* kept it must always appear; and with the setting presented by *ʻo* it appears as well.
options.explanation: The place word can stand without it, as *ʻi le faʻatoʻaga sā galue le tama* shows.

options.label: C
options.text: It stands after the verb; with the place word *ʻi* kept it is normal but can be left out; and with the setting presented by *ʻo* it appears as well.
options.explanation: Correct: the pointing-back word is normal but not compulsory after a phrase with *ʻi*, and it appears in *ʻO le faʻatoʻaga sā galue ai le tama* as well.

options.label: D
options.text: It stands after the verb; with the place word *ʻi* kept it is normal but can be left out; and with the setting presented by *ʻo* it is left out, since *ʻo* has taken the place word's place.
options.explanation: The setting presented by *ʻo* is still answered by the pointing-back word, as *ʻO le faʻatoʻaga sā galue ai le tama* shows.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the order of the naming sentence are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Both orders are good Samoan and say the same thing, and which one a speaker picks is largely free.
options.explanation: True: *ʻO se uō le tama* and *ʻO le tama ʻo se uō* both say "The boy is a friend".

options.label: B
options.text: When the part being named is a demonstrative such as *lenā*, it can come first or second.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because a demonstrative must come second, as in *ʻO le faleoʻo lenā*.

options.label: C
options.text: The naming part nearly always carries *ʻo*, while the part being named carries *ʻo* only when it comes first.
options.explanation: True: that is why *ʻO le tama ʻo se uō* carries *ʻo* twice.

options.label: D
options.text: When the part being named is the speaker, it comes first.
options.explanation: True: that is why the chapter says *ʻO aʻu ʻo se uō* for "I am a friend".

questions.prompt: In the le-phrase *le nofo*, what is each of the two words doing?

options.label: A
options.text: *le* is the article, setting the event in time the way a tense particle does; *nofo* is still the verb for staying.
options.explanation: The second half is right, but the article does not set the event in time: it packs the event into a thing.

options.label: B
options.text: *le* is the article, packing the event into a thing; *nofo* is still the verb for staying.
options.explanation: Correct: the article packs the event into a thing, and *nofo* is still the verb *nofo*, keeping its own meaning.

options.label: C
options.text: *le* is the article, setting the event in time the way a tense particle does; *nofo* has turned into a different word, a noun with a meaning of its own.
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: the article packs the event into a thing rather than setting its time, and *nofo* keeps its own meaning as a verb.

options.label: D
options.text: *le* is the article, packing the event into a thing; *nofo* has turned into a different word, a noun with a meaning of its own.
options.explanation: The first half is right, but *nofo* is still the verb *nofo*; only the article in front of it has changed what the phrase can do.

questions.prompt: What do the words *manatu* and *manava* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: think; feel lonely, and school
options.explanation: The first is right, but *manava* is the stomach, not a school.

options.label: B
options.text: stomach, and think; feel lonely
options.explanation: These are the right two meanings in the wrong order.

options.label: C
options.text: waste, and stomach
options.explanation: The second is right, but *manatu* means think; feel lonely, not waste.

options.label: D
options.text: think; feel lonely, and stomach
options.explanation: Correct: *manatu* is think; feel lonely, and *manava* is the stomach.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the le-phrase are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: A tense particle can stand inside it, between the article and the verb.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: a le-phrase never carries a tense particle anywhere inside it.

options.label: B
options.text: The article comes first and the verb after it, always in that order.
options.explanation: True: the article *le* comes first and the verb follows it, in a fixed order.

options.label: C
options.text: When it carries the not-word *lē*, the not-word stands between the article and the verb.
options.explanation: True: the not-word takes the middle place, as in *le lē fiafia*.

options.label: D
options.text: A verb inside it that has a plural shape takes that shape when what the phrase is about is more than one.
options.explanation: True: the verb inside still marks number, so the staying of more than one is *le nonofo*, not *le nofo*.

questions.prompt: In *le lē fiafia*, the article *le* and the not-word *lē* stand side by side. What tells them apart in writing, and how does most Samoan print handle the difference?

options.label: A
options.text: The long-vowel mark alone tells them apart; most Samoan print keeps the mark on the not-word, so the two never look alike.
options.explanation: The first half is right, but most Samoan print drops the marks, so the two are written alike.

options.label: B
options.text: The mark is decoration, and their place alone tells them apart; most Samoan print drops the marks and writes the two the same way, leaving the reader to take them apart by sense.
options.explanation: The second half is right, but the mark is not decoration: in writing it alone tells the two words apart.

options.label: C
options.text: The long-vowel mark alone tells them apart; most Samoan print drops the marks and writes the two the same way, leaving the reader to take them apart by sense.
options.explanation: Correct: the mark alone separates them in writing, and where print drops it, the reader tells them apart by sense.

options.label: D
options.text: The mark is decoration, and their place alone tells them apart; most Samoan print keeps the mark on the not-word, so the two never look alike.
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: the mark alone tells them apart in writing, and most Samoan print drops it.

questions.prompt: How do you say "the not being tired" in Samoan?

options.label: A
options.text: *le lē fiafia*

options.label: B

options.explanation: The verb is right, but without the not-word this is the being tired.

options.label: C

options.label: D
options.text: *le lē vāivai*

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the do-not verbs *ʻaua* and *sōia* are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻAua* forbids an action.
options.explanation: True: *ʻaua* forbids an action.

options.label: B
options.text: *Sōia* stops an action that is already under way.
options.explanation: True: *sōia* stops what has already started.

options.label: C
options.text: *Sōia* cannot be followed by a le-phrase.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: both do-not verbs take a le-phrase the same way, as in *Sōia le maumau=ina le taimi.*

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻAua* can be followed by a le-phrase whose verb has nothing after it, as in *ʻAua le nofo.*
options.explanation: True: the verb inside the phrase can stand with nothing after it; the sentence means Do not stay.

questions.prompt: What does *Sōia le maumau=ina le taimi.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Stop wasting time.
options.explanation: Correct: *sōia* stops what is under way, and *māumau* is waste, here in its long form.

options.label: B
options.text: Do not waste time.
options.explanation: The verb inside is right, but *sōia* stops an action already under way; forbidding one is the job of *ʻaua*.

options.label: C
options.text: Stop counting the time.
options.explanation: The stop verb is right, but *māumau* means waste, not count.

options.label: D
options.text: Do not count the time.
options.explanation: Neither part fits: *sōia* stops what is under way, and *māumau* means waste.

questions.prompt: What does *ʻAua le nonofo teine ʻi le āʻoga.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The girl should not stay at home.
options.explanation: Neither part fits: *nonofo* is the plural shape, so the girls are more than one, and *āʻoga* is school.

options.label: B
options.text: The girls should not stay at the school.
options.explanation: Correct: the plural *nonofo* shows the girls are more than one, and *āʻoga* is school.

options.label: C
options.text: The girls should not stay at home.
options.explanation: The number is right, but *āʻoga* is school, not home.

options.label: D
options.text: The girl should not stay at the school.
options.explanation: The place is right, but the verb inside is the plural *nonofo*, so the girls are more than one; for one girl it would be *nofo*.

questions.prompt: The phrase after *ma* in *Sā ʻou nofo ma le lē fiafia.* is a le-phrase. Which is true of it?

options.label: A
options.text: Only *ma* can mark a le-phrase, and after the place word *ʻi* only a plain noun phrase can stand; the not-word can stand in it because *fiafia* is still a verb, and it never stands in a phrase built on a noun.
options.explanation: The second half is right, but *ʻi* marks a le-phrase too: it goes wherever a noun phrase goes.

options.label: B
options.text: Only *ma* can mark a le-phrase, and after the place word *ʻi* only a plain noun phrase can stand; the not-word can stand in any phrase after an article, whether a verb or a noun follows it.
options.explanation: Both halves are wrong: a le-phrase goes after *ʻi* as well as *ma*, and the not-word stands in the middle only where a verb follows.

options.label: C
options.text: Like any noun phrase, a le-phrase can be marked by *ma*, as here, or by the place word *ʻi*; the not-word can stand in it because *fiafia* is still a verb, and it never stands in a phrase built on a noun.
options.explanation: Correct: the phrase is marked like any noun phrase, and the not-word fits because the middle word is still a verb.

options.label: D
options.text: Like any noun phrase, a le-phrase can be marked by *ma*, as here, or by the place word *ʻi*; the not-word can stand in any phrase after an article, whether a verb or a noun follows it.
options.explanation: The first half is right, but a noun in that middle slot never takes the not-word; only a verb does.

questions.prompt: How do you say "but" and "while" between two clauses, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: *ma* and *ʻaʻo*
options.explanation: The second is right, but the word for "but" is *ʻae*.

options.label: B

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻaʻo* and *ʻae*
options.explanation: These are the right two words in the wrong order.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻae* and *ma*
options.explanation: The first is right, but the word for "while" is *ʻaʻo*.

questions.prompt: Which tense particle goes in the gap? *Na taunuʻu mai le pasi ma ___ alu le teine ʻi le āʻoga.*

options.label: D

options.explanation: Correct: the particle in the clause after *ma* is the one already standing in front of the first clause, here *na*.

questions.prompt: What do *lolo*, *tuʻu* and *ana* mean, in that order?

options.explanation: The first and second are right, but *ana* means cave, not school.

questions.prompt: Which word goes in the gap so that the sentence says "It rained and the girl stayed in the cave"? *Sā timu ___ sā nofo le teine ʻi le ana.*

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻae*
options.explanation: The but-word would set the second clause against the first, and the English says "and".

options.label: B
options.text: *leʻi*
options.explanation: The not-yet word joins no two clauses on its own, and the English says "and".

options.label: C
options.text: *ma*
options.explanation: Correct: put between two clauses, *ma* joins them into one sentence and is read "and".

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻaʻo*
options.explanation: That word holds two events side by side and is read "while", and the English says "and".

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about joining two clauses with *ma* are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Two clauses joined by *ma* are usually heard as one thing after another in time.
options.explanation: True: *Sā timu ma sā lolo le vai* puts the rain first and the overflowing after it.

options.label: B
options.text: The matching of the tense particle holds even when the word straight after *ma* is a pointing phrase such as *ʻo lea* (then).
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because after a pointing phrase such as *ʻo lea* the clause takes whatever tense particle it needs, and no matching applies.

options.label: C
options.text: The two clauses *ma* joins can each be about a different person or thing.
options.explanation: True: each clause names its own, and *ma* joins them all the same.

options.label: D
options.text: The clause after *ma* can go without a tense particle altogether, and the sentence is still good Samoan.
options.explanation: True: *Sā timu ma lolo le vai* leaves that slot empty, and the empty slot is a form rather than a gap.

questions.prompt: What does *ʻUa ala le tama ma ʻua usu le teine.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The boy has woken and the girl has stood up.

options.label: C
options.text: The boy has sat down and the girl has stood up.
options.explanation: The second half is right, but *ala* means be awake, wake up, not sit down.

options.label: D

options.explanation: The first half is right, but *usu* means rise, stand up, not sit down.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about *ʻae* and *ʻaʻo* are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻAe* opens the second of the two clauses it joins, and never the first.
options.explanation: True: in *Sā ʻou nofo ʻae sā alu le teine* the but-word stands at the head of the second clause, the only place it takes.

options.label: B
options.text: The general particle *e* does not stand straight after *ʻae*: the two run together, and what you see is *ʻae* alone.
options.explanation: True: every other tense particle can follow *ʻae*, but this one is swallowed into it.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻAʻo* can open only the second of the two clauses, never the first.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because *ʻaʻo* can open either clause, and *ʻAʻo ʻou alu atu ʻi le āʻoga, sā ʻou mānatunatu ʻi le teine* opens on it.

options.label: D
options.text: In this chapter's sentences, the *ʻo* inside *ʻaʻo* is the short form of the happening-now particle *ʻoloʻo*.
options.explanation: True: *ʻaʻo* here is two words run together, and the second of them is that short form.

questions.prompt: What do *Na taunuʻu mai le pasi ʻaʻo leʻi tā=ina le ono.* and *Na taunuʻu mai le pasi ʻae leʻi tā=ina le ono.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: Both mean "The bus left before six o'clock."
options.explanation: The two sentences do mean the same thing, but *taunuʻu* means arrive, reach, not leave.

options.label: B
options.text: Both mean "The bus arrived before six o'clock."
options.explanation: Correct: the not-yet word straight after *ʻaʻo* or after *ʻae* says that the first thing happened before the second, and either combination does the work.

options.label: C
options.text: Both mean "The bus arrived after six o'clock."
options.explanation: In this *leʻi* ("not yet") pattern, the second clause reports what had not happened yet, so the bus came first: before six, not after.

options.label: D
options.text: The first means "The bus arrived before six o'clock", and the second "The bus arrived after six o'clock."
options.explanation: The first is right, but the second means the same as the first: *ʻae leʻi* says "before" just as *ʻaʻo leʻi* does.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about this chapter's joining words are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: When a preverbal pronoun stands between *ʻae* and *leʻi*, the general particle keeps its *e* shape.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because after a preverbal pronoun the general particle takes its *te* shape, as in *Na sele laʻu ʻava ʻae ʻou te leʻi tuʻu=a loʻu fale*, where it sits between *ʻou* and *leʻi*.

options.label: B
options.text: Whether the clause after *ma* repeats the tense particle or leaves its slot empty is a matter of style rather than of meaning.
options.explanation: True: *Sā timu ma sā lolo le vai* and *Sā timu ma lolo le vai* both say "It rained and the water overflowed".

options.label: C
options.text: The *ʻa* in *ʻaʻo* is the partner of the but-word, close to *ʻae* in meaning.
options.explanation: True: the two are near in meaning and differ in where they may stand.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻAe* sets the clause it opens against the one before it, so the two are heard as a contrast.
options.explanation: True: that contrast is why *ʻae* is called the but-word.

options.text: *ona*, and *loa*

options.label: C
options.text: *ona*, and *ai*
options.explanation: The first word is right, but *ai* is the pointing-back word, not the then-word.

options.label: D
options.text: *ai*, and *loa*
options.explanation: The second word is right, but *ai* is the pointing-back word, and it does not open the construction.

questions.prompt: What does *Na mātou mālōlō loa, mātou tāʻaʻalo ʻi le fale=ʻapa* mean?

questions.prompt: How do you say "Then the river overflowed" in the full shape of the then-construction?

options.label: A
options.text: *Ona lolo le vaitafe.*

options.text: *Ona lolo le ʻeleʻele.*

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the shapes of the then-construction are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Spoken Samoan can drop either *ona* or *lea*, and the clause still marks the next thing that happened.
options.explanation: True: with either word dropped, the one left carries the succession on its own.

options.label: B
options.text: After *lea*, what the clause names often has the presenting particle *ʻo* in front of it, and it can also stand in its plain form.
options.explanation: True: the presenting particle is often there after *lea*, but it is not required.

options.label: C
options.text: Modern writing and the Samoan of the Bible keep the full shape.
options.explanation: True: there the construction is always *ona*, the verb phrase, *lea*, then the rest of the clause.

options.label: D
options.text: With *lea* dropped, what the clause names keeps the presenting particle *ʻo* in front of it.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because with *lea* gone what the clause names stands in its plain form, as in *Ona alu le tama.*

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about how the then-construction is used are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: A text can open with a then-construction, since each one can stand as a sentence of its own.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because a then-construction reports what happened next, so a text never opens with one.

options.label: B
options.text: It is typical of storytelling: very frequent in spoken narrative, and virtually never heard in a formal speech.
options.explanation: True: it belongs to the telling of stories, and a formal speech virtually never uses it.

options.label: C
options.text: Putting the then-word *loa* inside a then-construction changes the meaning little, if at all.
options.explanation: True: the construction already carries the succession, so the English comes out the same with *loa* or without it.

options.label: D
options.text: The then-word *loa* can carry the succession by itself, with no *ona* and no *lea*.
options.explanation: True: in *Na mātou mālōlō loa*, "We then rested", the word *loa* alone says "then".

questions.prompt: In *ʻUa lilo atu ʻi le toga lālā le teine, ona oso ai lea ʻi lalo le tama*, what does *ai* reach back to?

options.label: A
options.text: The branches the girl hid in.
options.explanation: Reaching back to a place is the job it was met doing earlier; inside the then-construction it reaches wider.

options.label: B
options.text: The girl who hid.
options.explanation: It does not usually reach back to one word or one phrase here, and the girl is only part of what came before.

options.label: C
options.text: The hiding, and everything the story has said up to that point.
options.explanation: Correct: inside the then-construction it reaches back to the whole of what has been said before it.

options.label: D
options.text: The boy who jumped down.
options.explanation: The boy is named after it, in its own clause, and it points back, not forward.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about words and marks in this chapter are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: In *Sā ʻou alu loa ʻi fafo, ʻou fufulu oʻu mata*, the forms *ʻou* and *oʻu* are two spellings of one word meaning "I".
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because *ʻou* is the preverbal pronoun "I", while *oʻu*, with the mark after the vowel, says whose the eyes are.

options.label: B
options.text: In *fale=ʻapa* the equals sign joins two nouns into a single compound noun, and it is not the equals sign met on a long-form verb.
options.explanation: True: *fale* names the house and *ʻapa* says what its roof is made of.

options.label: C
options.text: In *le toga lālā*, the word *toga* means a cluster, a second meaning beside the direction it named earlier.
options.explanation: True: *lālā*, branch, follows it and says what the cluster is of.

options.label: D
options.text: In *Ona alu lea ʻo le tama*, the presenting particle *ʻo* stands in front of what the clause names.
options.explanation: True: *ʻo le tama* names the boy, and *ʻo* stands at its front.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about clauses that carry no tense particle are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: In *Na alu le tama, oso le teine ʻi le sami*, the *na* in front of the first clause sets the past for the second clause as well.
options.explanation: True: one tense particle at the front reaches over the whole run, so the jumping is past too.

options.label: B
options.text: Leaving the tense slot of the second clause empty says its event followed straight on from the first, or happened at the same time.
options.explanation: True: the empty slot is what ties the two clauses together.

options.label: C
options.text: The time a tense particle sets can reach on past a full stop into the next sentence.
options.explanation: True: a run of clauses does not have to stop where the full stop does.

options.label: D
options.text: In *Sā ʻou alu loa ʻi fafo. Fufulu oʻu mata.*, the second sentence names no one who washed, so who did it is left open.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because the *ʻou* of the first sentence says who washed, just as *sā* says when.

questions.prompt: What do the words *galo* and *tilotilo* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: watch or look, and forget
options.explanation: These are the right two meanings in the wrong order.

options.label: B
options.text: forget, and watch or look
options.explanation: Correct: *galo* is forget, and *tilotilo* is watch or look.

options.label: C
options.text: lie down, and watch or look
options.explanation: Lying down is *taʻatia*; the word *galo* is forget.

options.label: D
options.text: forget, and speak
options.explanation: Speaking is *tautala*; the word *tilotilo* is watch or look.

questions.prompt: Three of these words are paired with the meaning this chapter gives them. Which pairing is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻata*: laugh
options.explanation: The word *ʻata* does mean laugh, so this pairing is right.

options.label: B
options.text: *punou*: bend down
options.explanation: The word *punou* does mean bend down, so this pairing is right.

options.label: C
options.text: *mālūlū*: cool
options.explanation: The word *mālūlū* does mean cool, so this pairing is right.

options.label: D
options.text: *lē iloa*: bring
