options.explanation: Correct: *lē iloa* means lose or be lost; bringing is *ʻaumai*.

questions.prompt: What does *E leʻi mafai ona ʻou alu leaga sā timu.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: I could not go, and the rain was bad.
options.explanation: Here *leaga* is not used as the word for bad but as a because-word, opening the reason for what was just said.

options.label: B
options.text: I could not go because luckily it was raining.
options.explanation: The word *leaga* opens a reason that is a bad or unwelcome thing, so the reason cannot be a lucky one.

options.label: C
options.text: I could not go because unfortunately it was raining.
options.explanation: Correct: *leaga* opens the reason, and the reason is an unwelcome one, which the word unfortunately carries.

options.label: D
options.text: Unfortunately it rained because I could not go.
options.explanation: The because-word opens the reason for what was just said, so the rain is the reason and the not going is what it explains.

questions.prompt: Which sentence means "The boy went to bring the coconut"?

options.label: A
options.text: *Sā alu le tama e ʻaumai le niu.*
options.explanation: Correct: the general particle *e* heads the purpose clause, which says what the going was for.

options.label: B
options.text: *Sā alu le tama neʻi ʻaumai le niu.*
options.explanation: With *neʻi* at its head the purpose is a negative one, so this says the boy went so that he would not bring the coconut.

options.label: C
options.text: *Na alu le tama ʻi le fale ʻona ʻua maʻi le teine.*
options.explanation: This says the boy went to the house because the girl was sick, which gives a reason rather than a purpose.

options.label: D
options.text: *Sā ʻou alu neʻi tagi le tama.*
options.explanation: This says I went, so that the boy would not cry.

questions.prompt: Which of these is true of the because-words and the clauses they open?

options.label: A
options.text: The word *ʻona* always comes after the main clause and never opens the sentence; when a reason is put first, the other clause usually carries *ai* after its verb; and a reason clause with a verb in it carries a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: The word *ʻona* can also go first, as in *ʻOna ʻua maʻi le teine, na alu ai le tama ʻi le fale.*

options.label: B
options.text: The word *ʻona* can open the sentence, in front of the main clause; when a reason is put first, the other clause usually carries *ai* after its verb; and a reason clause with a verb in it takes no tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: The reason clause carries a tense particle of its own, as *ʻua* does in *ʻua vāivai*.

options.label: C
options.text: The word *ʻona* can open the sentence, in front of the main clause; when a reason is put first, the other clause stays exactly as it would be, with nothing added; and a reason clause with a verb in it carries a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: When a reason goes first, the other clause usually carries the pointing-back word *ai* after its verb, reaching back to the whole reason.

options.label: D
options.text: The word *ʻona* can open the sentence, in front of the main clause; when a reason is put first, the other clause usually carries *ai* after its verb; and a reason clause with a verb in it carries a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻona* can go first, the other clause then usually takes *ai*, and the reason clause carries its own tense particle.

questions.prompt: Three of these words are paired with the meaning this chapter gives them. Which pairing is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: *mālamalama*: understand; daylight
options.explanation: The word *mālamalama* does mean understand, and daylight as well, so this pairing is right.

options.label: B
options.text: *suga*: the word you call out to a girl
options.explanation: The word *suga* is the word you call out to a girl, so this pairing is right.

options.label: C
options.text: *moli*: the orange only; on its own it never means soap
options.explanation: Correct: on its own *moli* covers soap and the orange both, and the compound *fasimoli* is the word for a piece of soap.

options.label: D
options.text: *siʻi*: move
options.explanation: The word *siʻi* does mean move, so this pairing is right.

questions.prompt: Which of these is how this chapter tells you to read *ona* and *ʻona*?

options.label: A
options.text: A tense particle in front of the verb that follows marks the because-word, and no tense particle marks the that-word; the *ona* of the then-construction is told from the that-word by the *lea* that trails it; and before a noun phrase the because-word takes the presenting particle *ʻo*.
options.explanation: Correct: the tense particle sorts the because-word from the that-word, the trailing *lea* sorts out the then-construction, and *ʻo* stands between *ʻona* and a noun phrase.

options.label: B
options.text: The ʻ mark marks the because-word, and ordinary Samoan writing always prints it, so the mark is the test; the *ona* of the then-construction is told from the that-word by the *lea* that trails it; and before a noun phrase the because-word takes the presenting particle *ʻo*.
options.explanation: In ordinary Samoan the two are usually both written *ona*, so the tense particle is the test to use.

options.label: C
options.text: A tense particle in front of the verb that follows marks the because-word, and no tense particle marks the that-word; the *ona* of the then-construction is told from the that-word by a tense particle in front of its verb; and before a noun phrase the because-word takes the presenting particle *ʻo*.
options.explanation: The verb after the *ona* of the then-construction carries no tense particle either, so the trailing *lea* is what tells it apart.

options.label: D
options.text: A tense particle in front of the verb that follows marks the because-word, and no tense particle marks the that-word; the *ona* of the then-construction is told from the that-word by the *lea* that trails it; and before a noun phrase the because-word stands straight in front of it, with nothing between.
options.explanation: Before a noun phrase *ʻona* takes the presenting particle, as in *ʻona ʻo le timu*.

questions.prompt: Which particle fills the gap in *Sā ʻou alu ʻou ___ ʻaumai le niu.* ("I went to bring the coconut.")?

options.label: A
options.explanation: After a preverbal pronoun such as *ʻou* the general particle does not stay *e*; it takes its other shape.

options.label: B
options.text: *neʻi*
options.explanation: With *neʻi* the purpose would be a negative one, and the English says the going was to bring the coconut.

options.label: C
options.text: *te*
options.explanation: Correct: after a preverbal pronoun the general particle takes the shape *te*, so *ʻou te* heads the purpose clause.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻauā*
options.explanation: The word *ʻauā* is a because-word, and it opens a reason rather than a purpose.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: A purpose clause headed by the general particle needs no joining word: it follows the main clause directly.
options.explanation: This is true: no joining word attaches a purpose clause headed by the general particle, and it follows the main clause directly.

options.label: B
options.text: In the full why-question this chapter teaches, *ʻaiseā* stands at the end of its clause, and nothing in the verb phrase points back to it.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: in the full question *ʻaiseā* stands at the front of its clause, and *ai* in the verb phrase points back to it.

options.label: C
options.text: Besides the general particle, the mood particle *ʻia* can also head a purpose clause.
options.explanation: This is true: a purpose clause can also be headed by *ʻia* in place of the general particle.

options.label: D
options.text: A negative purpose clause can leave out the thing that is not to be noticed, when a sentence before it has already named that thing.
options.explanation: This is true: in *ʻUa ʻou ʻata ma ʻou punou ʻi lalo neʻi iloa mai e le tama.* the watching is not named again, because the sentence before it named it.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: A reason clause opened by *leaga* belongs to everyday speech, and you will seldom meet the word doing this job in writing or formal language.
options.explanation: This is true: the because-word *leaga* belongs to everyday speech and is seldom met in writing or formal language.

options.label: B
options.text: The word *ʻaiseā* is used mainly on its own, as the one-word question, and the full why-sentence is heard in more formal language.
options.explanation: This is true: *ʻAiseā?* on its own is the usual question, and the full sentence belongs to more formal language.

options.label: C
options.text: A because-word and its reason can stand as the whole answer to a why-question, with no main clause of their own.
options.explanation: This is true: *ʻAuā ʻua maʻi le teine.* can be the whole of an answer.

options.label: D
options.text: A clause opened by *ʻauā* goes in front of the main clause as freely as a clause opened by *ʻona*.
options.explanation: Correct, this is the false one: a clause opened by *ʻauā* normally comes after the main clause, and putting it first is rare.

questions.prompt: Which word is the if-word, and which word can open a condition clause at the head of a sentence with no if-word in front of it, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻāfai*, then *ʻoleʻā*
options.explanation: The if-word is right, but a condition with no joining word opens on the short form of the future particle, not on its full form *ʻoleʻā*.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻā*, then *ʻāfai*
options.explanation: These are the right two words in the wrong order: *ʻāfai* is the if-word, and *ʻā* is the one that needs no if-word.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻāfai*, then *ʻā*
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻāfai* is the if-word, and *ʻā*, the short form of the future particle, opens a condition clause with no joining word in front of it.

options.label: D
options.text: *pē*, then *ʻā*
options.explanation: The second word is right, but *pē* is the question opener, and the if-word is *ʻāfai*.

questions.prompt: Three of these words are paired with the meaning this chapter gives them. Which pairing is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: *apu*: apple
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *apu* means apple.

options.label: B
options.text: *solo*: rope
options.explanation: Correct: *solo* means towel, not rope.

options.label: C
options.text: *uosi*: waltz
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *uosi* means waltz.

options.label: D
options.text: *silou*: slow
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *silou* means slow.

questions.prompt: The chapter teaches *mālaia* and *pōloaʻiga*. What do they mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: disaster, and answer
options.explanation: The first is right, but *pōloaʻiga* means instruction.

options.label: B
options.text: instruction, and disaster
options.explanation: These are the right two meanings in the wrong order.

options.label: C
options.text: celebration, and instruction
options.explanation: The second is right, but *mālaia* means disaster.

options.label: D
options.text: disaster, and instruction
options.explanation: Correct: *mālaia* means disaster and *pōloaʻiga* means instruction.

questions.prompt: What does *ʻĀfai e mālosi le loto o le tama, e lē usitaʻi* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: If the boy's will is strong, he does not obey.
options.explanation: Correct: the if-word opens the condition, *loto* is the will, and *usitaʻi* is obey, here under the not-word.

options.label: B
options.text: If the boy's voice is strong, he does not obey.
options.explanation: The word *loto* means will or heart, not voice.

options.label: C
options.text: If the boy's will is strong, he does not sleep.
options.explanation: The word *usitaʻi* means obey, not sleep.

options.label: D
options.text: If the boy does not obey, his will is strong.
options.explanation: The condition is the clause the if-word opens, the boy's strong will, and not obeying is what follows from it.

questions.prompt: What does *ʻĀ ʻe alu ʻi le matāfaga, ʻaumai le solo* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: When you go to the market, you bring the towel.
options.explanation: Both halves are off: *matāfaga* is the beach, and *ʻaumai le solo* is a command, "bring the towel".

options.label: B
options.text: When you go to the beach, bring the towel.
options.explanation: Correct: *matāfaga* is the beach, and the main clause behind the condition is a command.

options.label: C
options.text: When you go to the market, bring the towel.
options.explanation: The command is right, but *matāfaga* is the beach.

options.label: D
options.text: When you go to the beach, you bring the towel.
options.explanation: The place is right, but the main clause *ʻaumai le solo* is a command, "bring the towel", and not a statement of what you do.

questions.prompt: What does *E lē alu le malaga pē ʻā afā* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: There will be no trip, whether or not there is a storm.
options.explanation: Here the clause after *pē* is a condition, not the whether of a reported question.

options.label: B
options.text: There will be no trip, whether or not there is a fire.
options.explanation: Both halves are off: the clause after *pē* is a condition, "when there is a storm", and *afā* is a storm, not a fire.

options.label: C
options.text: There will be no trip when there is a fire.
options.explanation: The shape is right, but *afā* is a storm.

options.label: D
options.text: There will be no trip when there is a storm.
options.explanation: Correct: the clause after *pē* is a condition, and *afā* is a storm.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is a correct Samoan way to say "If it rains tomorrow, the trip will not go"?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻĀ e timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga.*
options.explanation: The short future particle is itself the tense particle of its clause, so a second one, *e*, has no place behind it.

options.label: B
options.text: *E lē alu le malaga ʻāfai e timu taeao.*
options.explanation: A condition clause that follows the main clause takes the question opener in front of it, so this needs *pē ʻāfai*.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻĀfai e timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga.*
options.explanation: Correct: the if-word opens the condition, its verb *timu* carries the general particle *e*, and the main clause follows the comma.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻĀfai timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga.*
options.explanation: The clause after the if-word has a verb, *timu*, and a verb there carries a tense particle of its own, which is missing here.

questions.prompt: In *ʻĀfai ʻua sau le tama, ʻoleʻā alu le teine* and *ʻĀfai ʻoleʻā timu taeao, e lē alu le malaga*, what does the tense particle of each condition say about it, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: In the first, that the speaker is not sure it will come true; in the second, that it is much more certain than under the general particle, as something expected soon.
options.explanation: The second is right, but *ʻua* presents the condition as something new that has come about; not being sure is a reading of the general particle *e*.

options.label: B
options.text: In the first, that it is something new that has come about; in the second, that it is much more certain than under the general particle, as something expected soon.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻua* presents the condition as something new that has come about, and *ʻoleʻā* points at something expected to happen soon.

options.label: C
options.text: In the first, that it is much more certain than under the general particle; in the second, that it is something new that has come about.
options.explanation: These are the right two readings in the wrong order: *ʻua* is the one for something new, and *ʻoleʻā* the one for greater certainty.

options.label: D
options.text: In the first, that it is something new that has come about; in the second, that it is less certain than under the general particle, though still something expected soon.
options.explanation: The first is right, but *ʻoleʻā* carries a much higher degree of certainty than the general particle does, not a lower one.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about condition clauses are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: A clause opened by *ʻā* only ever looks ahead to something still to come, never back into the past.
options.explanation: Correct: the shape can also look back into the past, as in *ʻĀ fānau mai le ulugāliʻi, e fiafia le ʻāiga*, "When the couple had children, the family was happy".

options.label: B
options.text: A naming sentence opened by *ʻo* can stand as the condition, with no verb in it at all.
options.explanation: This is true: *ʻĀfai ʻo le tonu, ʻua lelei* has a naming sentence as its condition.

options.label: C
options.text: Under the general particle *e*, one Samoan condition can mean that the speaker is not sure it will come true, or can mean "whenever" it is given.
options.explanation: This is true: *ʻĀfai e timu, e lē alu le malaga* carries both readings, and nothing in the Samoan chooses between them.

options.label: D
options.text: A condition clause standing in front of the main clause is occasionally opened by *pē* as well.
options.explanation: This is true, though the usual shape has nothing in front of the if-word or the short future particle.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the particles of this chapter are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: Samoan does not mark whether a clause opened by *ʻā* means "if", "when" or "whenever", so the choice among the three English words is the translator's.
options.explanation: This is true: the Samoan is the same whichever English word fits how expected the condition is.

options.label: B
options.text: The short future particle has a second written shape, *ʻa*, and what decides between the two shapes is not known.
options.explanation: This is true: mostly the two look like free alternatives.

options.label: C
options.text: After *pē*, the short future particle is written only as *ʻā*.
options.explanation: This is true: after the question opener only the long shape appears, as in *E lē alu le malaga pē ʻā afā*.

options.label: D
options.text: This chapter teaches *ʻā* as a fourth tense particle that can stand behind *ʻāfai*, beside *e*, *ʻua* and *ʻoleʻā*.
options.explanation: Correct: behind the if-word this chapter teaches three tense particles, and *ʻā* belongs to the other shape, standing where the if-word and its tense particle would be.

questions.prompt: Which word is the verb for having plenty, and which is the verb for listening, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: *tau*, and *faʻalogo*
options.explanation: The word *tau* is cost or price; the verb for listening is right.

options.label: B
options.text: *faʻalogo*, and *mau*
options.explanation: These are the right two words in the wrong order.

options.label: C
options.text: *mau*, and *faʻalogo*
options.explanation: Correct: *mau* is to have plenty and *faʻalogo* is to listen or hear, and each is the base of two words this chapter builds.

options.label: D
options.text: *mau*, and *fai*
options.explanation: The verb *fai* is do, make, say or tell; the verb for having plenty is right.

questions.prompt: Three of these are paired with the meaning or job this chapter gives them. Which pairing is wrong?

options.label: A
options.text: *taugōfie*: expensive
options.explanation: Correct: this is the wrong pairing, because *taugōfie* carries the easy ending and is not the expensive word.

options.label: B
options.text: *faigatā*: difficult
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *faigatā* means difficult.

options.label: C
options.text: *=gōfie*: the ending that builds an easy-word
options.explanation: This pairing is right: that is the job of *=gōfie*.

options.label: D
options.text: *maugōfie*: generous
options.explanation: This pairing is right: *maugōfie* means generous.

questions.prompt: Which phrase means "the mean person"?

options.label: A
options.text: *le tagata faʻalogogatā*
options.explanation: This describing word is built on *faʻalogo*, listening, not on *mau*.

options.label: B
options.text: *le tagata maugōfie*
options.explanation: This one is built on *mau* with the other ending, and it is not the mean word.

options.label: C
options.text: *le tama faʻalogogōfie*
options.explanation: Here the noun is *tama*, a boy, and the describing word is built on *faʻalogo*, not on *mau*.

options.label: D
options.text: *le tagata maugatā*
options.explanation: Correct: *maugatā* means mean or tight-fisted, so this is the mean person.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about a describing word inside a noun phrase are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: It is still a verb there, the same word that can be the verb of a sentence.
options.explanation: This is true: a describing word does not change class, whichever position it stands in.

options.label: B
options.text: When the noun has no article and means more than one, the describing word keeps its singular form.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because in *pusi uli* the describing word takes its plural form, *uli*.

options.label: C
options.text: The noun it describes can be the place where the action happens, as the room is in *ʻO le potu moe*.
options.explanation: This is true: *ʻO le potu moe* is a bedroom, where the room is the place of the sleeping and not the one who sleeps.

options.label: D
options.text: It can carry a place phrase with it, and the whole of it still fills the one describing slot, as in *le pasi alu ʻi le nuʻu*.
options.explanation: This is true: the going and the village it goes to stand together in the one slot.

questions.prompt: What does *le tagata faʻalogogatā* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: the person who is easy to hear
options.explanation: That adds up the parts of the word, and takes the other ending's meaning as well.

options.label: B
options.text: the person who is hard to hear
options.explanation: That is the sum of the two parts, and a built word's meaning is learned as a word of its own.

options.label: C
options.text: the disobedient person
options.explanation: Correct: *faʻalogogatā* means disobedient, not hard to hear.

options.label: D
options.text: the obedient person
options.explanation: Obedient is the opposite of what this word means.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the two compounds this chapter teaches are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: In a verb-and-noun compound, the noun behind the verb has an article in front of it, like a noun in a sentence.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because the noun stands bare, with no article, as *umu* does in *le teine fai umu*.

options.label: B
options.text: A part-and-quality compound such as *isu mamafa* works as one describing verb: it can be the verb of a sentence, and it can describe a noun inside a noun phrase.
options.explanation: This is true: *isu mamafa* is the verb of the sentence for having a cold, and *tino leaga* describes the people in *tagata tino leaga*.

options.label: C
options.text: The noun a verb-and-noun compound describes can be the one doing the action, the place it happens in, or the thing it is done with.
options.explanation: This is true: in *le teine fai umu* it is the girl who does it, and in other compounds it can be the place or the thing used.

options.label: D
options.text: The verb inside a verb-and-noun compound usually keeps its short form, and the long-form ending is rare there.
options.explanation: This is true: the short form is the usual one in that position.

questions.prompt: The chapter teaches *faigōfie*, *taugatā* and *faʻalogogōfie*. What do they mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: difficult, expensive, obedient
options.explanation: The first is wrong: *faigōfie* means easy.

options.label: B
options.text: easy, cheap, obedient
options.explanation: The second is wrong: *taugatā* means expensive.

options.label: C
options.text: easy, expensive, disobedient
options.explanation: The third is wrong: *faʻalogogōfie* means obedient.

options.label: D
options.text: easy, expensive, obedient
options.explanation: Correct: *faigōfie* is easy, *taugatā* is expensive and *faʻalogogōfie* is obedient.

questions.prompt: What does *le tagata loto vāivai ma le fefe* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The timid person is with the frightened one.
options.explanation: That reads *ma* as setting two people side by side in a sentence, but here it joins a second description to the one person.

options.label: B
options.text: the timid and frightened person
options.explanation: Correct: *ma* joins *le fefe*, the being afraid, to the description of the same one person.

options.label: C
options.text: the timid person and the frightened person
options.explanation: There is only one person here, because what *ma* joins is *le fefe*, an article in front of a verb, not a second person.

options.label: D
options.text: The person is timid and frightened.
options.explanation: That is a statement about the person, and this is a noun phrase naming the person, with no tense particle in it.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about the Samoan noun phrase are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: The article comes first, then the name of the thing, then the describing verb.
options.explanation: This is true: *le taʻavale uliuli* is the article, then the car, then black.

options.label: B
options.text: More than one describing verb can stand on one noun, one behind the other, with no joining word between them.
options.explanation: This is true: *paʻepaʻe* and *mānaia* stand side by side in *le pusa paʻepaʻe mānaia*.

options.label: C
options.text: A describing verb agrees in number with the noun it describes whatever the relation between them, and this chapter states that rule for every relation.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because the chapter states the agreement only where the noun stands to the verb as a subject does in a sentence with a single participant, and states no rule past that.

options.label: D
options.text: A pointing word, when the phrase has one, comes after all its describing verbs.
options.explanation: This is true: *lenā* closes *le pusa paʻepaʻe mānaia lenā*, after both describing verbs.

questions.prompt: Three of these statements about this chapter's describing words and endings are true. Which one is false?

options.label: A
options.text: *=gatā* builds a difficult-word, and it can also stand on its own as a word meaning difficult.
options.explanation: Correct: this is the false one, because *=gatā* is never a word standing on its own; it always goes on another word.

options.label: B
options.text: The phrases *tagata tino leaga* and *tagata e tino leaga* do the same work, one without the general particle *e* and one with it.
options.explanation: This is true: the shorter phrase does the work of the longer one without the particle.

options.label: C
options.text: The words *=gatā* and *=gōfie* build are verbs, so they can describe a noun and can also be the verb of a sentence.
options.explanation: This is true: *le taʻavale taugatā* and *E faigatā le gagana* show both jobs.

options.label: D
options.text: Both *=gatā* and *=gōfie* can also go on a verb that already carries the long-form ending.
options.explanation: This is true, though this chapter builds its words from a plain verb only.

questions.prompt: In *Sā tatala e le teine le pusa.*, what does *e* mark, and what does a doer said as a preverbal pronoun take?

options.label: A
options.text: It is the agent marker in front of the doer phrase *e le teine*, and *le pusa*, the one the action happened to, stands bare; a doer said as a preverbal pronoun, in front of the verb, takes the agent marker as well.
options.explanation: The first half is right, but a doer said as a preverbal pronoun stands in front of the verb and takes no marker.

options.label: B
options.text: It marks *le teine* as the one the action happened to, and *le pusa*, standing bare, is the doer; a doer said as a preverbal pronoun, in front of the verb, takes no marker.
options.explanation: The agent marker goes in front of the doer, so the girl did the opening and the box, standing bare, is what was opened.

options.label: C
options.text: It is the agent marker in front of the doer phrase *e le teine*, and *le pusa*, the one the action happened to, stands bare; a doer said as a preverbal pronoun, in front of the verb, takes no marker.
options.explanation: Correct on both: the agent marker rides on the doer phrase after the verb, and a doer said as a preverbal pronoun carries no marker.

options.label: D
options.text: It marks *le teine* as the one the action happened to, and *le pusa*, standing bare, is the doer; a doer said as a preverbal pronoun, in front of the verb, takes the agent marker as well.
options.explanation: The roles are the other way round, and a doer said as a preverbal pronoun takes no marker either.

questions.prompt: In *ʻAua le tatala=ina le pusa lenā.*, which account of the le-phrase, the forbidding rule, and what else *ʻaua* can take agrees with the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: The *le* in *ʻaua le* is the article of a le-phrase, an event packed into a thing, and *sōia* takes a le-phrase the same way; forbidding with *ʻaua le* takes the long form, and speakers reject the short form there, though a few short forms turn up in print; *ʻaua* can also take the person and the general particle *te* before the verb.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: the le-phrase both do-not verbs can take, the forbidding rule that is firm without being exceptionless, and the second frame *ʻaua* can take.

options.label: B
options.text: The *le* in *ʻaua le* is the article of a le-phrase, an event packed into a thing, but only *ʻaua* takes one and *sōia* never does; forbidding with *ʻaua le* takes the long form, and speakers reject the short form there, though a few short forms turn up in print; *ʻaua* can also take the person and the general particle *te* before the verb.
options.explanation: The other do-not verb takes a le-phrase the same way, so *sōia* can stand in front of one just as *ʻaua* does.

options.label: C
options.text: The *le* in *ʻaua le* is the article of a le-phrase, an event packed into a thing, and *sōia* takes a le-phrase the same way; forbidding with *ʻaua le* takes the long form, and no short form turns up there at all, in speech or in print; *ʻaua* can also take the person and the general particle *te* before the verb.
options.explanation: Speakers reject the short form after *ʻaua le*, but a few short forms do turn up in print, which is why this rule is firm without being exceptionless.

options.label: D
options.text: The *le* in *ʻaua le* is the article of a le-phrase, an event packed into a thing, and *sōia* takes a le-phrase the same way; forbidding with *ʻaua le* takes the long form, and speakers reject the short form there, though a few short forms turn up in print; *ʻaua* always takes *le* after it, so the person and the general particle *te* cannot follow it.
options.explanation: The do-not verb can also take the person and *te* before the verb, as in the chapter's *ʻAua ʻe te siva*.

questions.prompt: Which of these gives "The boy killed the pig." with the boy put at the front, and states how firm the choice of verb form is?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻO le puaʻa sā tapē e le tama.* When the doer goes first the verb usually takes the long form, which is a tendency rather than a firm rule.
options.explanation: This line puts the pig first behind *ʻo*, with the boy still marked by *e* after the verb.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻO le tama sā tapē=ina le puaʻa.* When the doer goes first the verb must take the long form, which is a firm rule just like the two command rules.
options.explanation: The line is right, but the long form under a doer put first is a tendency, unlike the two command rules.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻO le puaʻa sā tapē e le tama.* When the doer goes first the verb must take the long form, which is a firm rule just like the two command rules.
options.explanation: This line puts the pig first, and the long form under a doer put first is only what speakers usually choose.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻO le tama sā tapē=ina le puaʻa.* When the doer goes first the verb usually takes the long form, which is a tendency rather than a firm rule.
options.explanation: Correct on both: the whole doer phrase stands behind *ʻo* with its old slot empty, and the long form there is a tendency.

questions.prompt: What does *Na iloa e loʻu ataliʻi ʻua sasae le ʻie.* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: My son knew that the cloth has been torn.
options.explanation: The report's *ʻua* is read against the time of the knowing, not the moment of speaking, so after a past knowing the English moves to "had been torn".

options.label: B
options.text: My son knew that the cloth had been torn.
options.explanation: Correct: no doer is named in the report, and its *ʻua* is read against the past knowing.

options.label: C
options.text: My son knew that he himself had torn the cloth.
options.explanation: No doer stands in the report and nothing takes its place, so the cloth is what was torn and nobody is named as tearing it.

options.label: D
options.text: My son knew that he has torn the cloth.
options.explanation: The report names no doer, and its *ʻua* is read against the past knowing, so the English is "the cloth had been torn".

questions.prompt: Read *Sā nofo le teine ʻi le ana ʻae sā alu le tama.*, *Na usu le tama ʻaʻo moe le teine.* and *Na alu le tama, oso le teine ʻi le sami.* Three claims: (1) the but-word *ʻae* can open the first of two contrasted clauses as well as the second; (2) *ʻaʻo* holds two events together in time, very often as "while", and can open either clause; (3) in a run of clauses sharing one tense particle, every later clause repeats that particle in front of it. Which of them need correcting?

options.label: A
options.text: Claim 1 only.
options.explanation: Claim 3 also needs correcting, because in such a run the slot in front of every later clause is left empty, as it is in front of *oso*.

options.label: B
options.text: Claims 1, 2 and 3.
options.explanation: Claim 2 stands as the chapter gives it: *ʻaʻo* holds two events together, very often as "while", and can open either clause.

options.label: C
options.text: Claims 1 and 3.
options.explanation: Correct: *ʻae* opens only the second of two contrasted clauses, and the later clauses of a run leave their tense-particle slot empty.

options.label: D
options.text: Claim 3 only.
options.explanation: Claim 1 also needs correcting, because the but-word *ʻae* opens the second of two contrasted clauses and never the first.

questions.prompt: Read *ʻUa mālamalama le teine ʻauā ʻua tautala le tama.* and *E lē mafai ona ʻe alu ʻona ʻo le timu.* Which account of the because-words agrees with the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: *Leaga* is the plain because-word and *ʻauā* gives a reason that is unwelcome; *ʻona* is the one that goes first freely, while putting *ʻauā* first is rare; after *ʻona ʻo* stands a noun phrase, *le timu*, with the presenting particle *ʻo* between it and *ʻona*.
options.explanation: The plain one is *ʻauā*, and *leaga* is the one that gives a reason that is unwelcome.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻAuā* is the plain because-word and *leaga* gives a reason that is unwelcome; *ʻauā* is the one that goes first freely, while putting *ʻona* first is rare; after *ʻona ʻo* stands a noun phrase, *le timu*, with the presenting particle *ʻo* between it and *ʻona*.
options.explanation: The because-word that goes first freely is *ʻona*, and putting *ʻauā* first is rare.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻAuā* is the plain because-word and *leaga* gives a reason that is unwelcome; *ʻona* is the one that goes first freely, while putting *ʻauā* first is rare; after *ʻona* stands a clause, *ʻo le timu*, keeping a tense particle of its own, as the clause after *ʻauā* does.
options.explanation: The *ʻo* is the presenting particle and *le timu* is a noun phrase, so *ʻona ʻo* means "because of" with no tense particle in it.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻAuā* is the plain because-word and *leaga* gives a reason that is unwelcome; *ʻona* is the one that goes first freely, while putting *ʻauā* first is rare; after *ʻona ʻo* stands a noun phrase, *le timu*, with the presenting particle *ʻo* between it and *ʻona*.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: the plain and the unwelcome reason, the because-word that goes first freely, and the noun phrase after *ʻona ʻo*.

questions.prompt: In *Sā alu le tama e ʻaumai le niu.* and *Sā ʻou alu neʻi tagi le tama.*, which account of the clause that follows each main clause is right?

options.label: A
options.text: In the first, *e* is the general particle heading a purpose clause that follows the main clause with no joining word; in the second, the warning particle *neʻi* takes that place because the action is done to prevent something.
options.explanation: Correct on both: the general particle heads the plain purpose clause, and *neʻi* heads it when the action is done to prevent something.

options.label: B
options.text: In the first, *e* is the agent marker, so what follows it names the one who did the going; in the second, the warning particle *neʻi* takes that place because the action is done to prevent something.
options.explanation: Here *e* stands in front of the verb *ʻaumai*, not in front of a doer phrase after the verb, so it heads a purpose clause.

options.label: C
options.text: In the first, *e* is the general particle heading a purpose clause that follows the main clause with no joining word; in the second, *neʻi* takes that place to say, as the not-word *lē* would, that the going itself did not happen.
options.explanation: The going did happen, and *neʻi* heads a clause saying what it was done to prevent.

options.label: D
options.text: In the first, *e* is the agent marker, so what follows it names the one who did the going; in the second, *neʻi* takes that place to say, as the not-word *lē* would, that the going itself did not happen.
options.explanation: The *e* in front of *ʻaumai* heads a purpose clause, and *neʻi* says what the going was done to prevent.

questions.prompt: Read *E sā ona ulaula.*, *E mālosi atu le tama i lo le teine.* and *E sili ona mālosi le maile.* Which account agrees with the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Only after *sā* does the that-word *ona* open the complement clause, while *mafai* and *tatau* take their clause with nothing joining it; comparison adds no ending to the quality word, *atu* after it raises the degree and *i lo* names what it is weighed against; *sili ona* in front of the quality word picks out the one that stands above the rest.
options.explanation: All three of *mafai*, *tatau* and *sā* take a complement clause, and after each of them *ona* opens it.

options.label: B
options.text: After *mafai*, *tatau* and *sā* the that-word *ona* opens the complement clause, which names the event while the word in front grades it; comparison adds no ending to the quality word, *atu* after it raises the degree and *i lo* names what it is weighed against; *sili ona* in front of the quality word picks out the one that stands above the rest.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: *ona* after the three grading words, *atu* and *i lo* in their two jobs, and *sili ona* for the one above the rest.

options.label: C
options.text: After *mafai*, *tatau* and *sā* the that-word *ona* opens the complement clause, which names the event while the word in front grades it; comparison adds no ending to the quality word, *i lo* raises the degree and *atu* names what it is weighed against; *sili ona* in front of the quality word picks out the one that stands above the rest.
options.explanation: The direction word *atu* after the quality word raises the degree, and the than-word *i lo* names what it is weighed against.

options.label: D
options.text: After *mafai*, *tatau* and *sā* the that-word *ona* opens the complement clause, which names the event while the word in front grades it; comparison adds no ending to the quality word, *atu* after it raises the degree and *i lo* names what it is weighed against; *sili ona* in front of the quality word weighs the dog against one other thing, as *atu* with *i lo* does.
options.explanation: The dog is not weighed against one other thing, because *sili ona* picks out the one that stands above the rest.

questions.prompt: In *ʻO le fale o le aliʻi.*, *ʻO le pusi ʻi lalo o le fale.* and *le pusi uliuli*, which account agrees with the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: In the first, the belonging word *o* marks a relationship the owner started and controls, where *a* marks one that is given; the second sets its spatial noun in a frame of four parts, the place word *ʻi*, the spatial noun, the belonging word *o*, then the thing the position is measured against; in the third the describing verb stands after the name of the thing and says which one is meant.
options.explanation: The two belonging words run the other way: *a* marks a relationship the owner started and controls, and *o* a given one, such as the house a person lives in.

options.label: B
options.text: In the first, the belonging word *o* marks a relationship that is given, such as the house a person lives in, where *a* marks one the owner started and controls; the second sets its spatial noun in a frame of four parts, the place word *ʻi*, the thing the position is measured against, the belonging word *o*, then the spatial noun; in the third the describing verb stands after the name of the thing and says which one is meant.
options.explanation: The spatial noun comes straight after *ʻi* and the thing the position is measured against comes last, as *lalo* and *le fale* do here.

options.label: C
options.text: In the first, the belonging word *o* marks a relationship that is given, such as the house a person lives in, where *a* marks one the owner started and controls; the second sets its spatial noun in a frame of four parts, the place word *ʻi*, the spatial noun, the belonging word *o*, then the thing the position is measured against; in the third the describing verb stands in front of the name of the thing and says which one is meant.
options.explanation: The describing verb follows the name of the thing: *pusi* names the cat, and *uliuli* after it says which cat is meant.

options.label: D
options.text: In the first, the belonging word *o* marks a relationship that is given, such as the house a person lives in, where *a* marks one the owner started and controls; the second sets its spatial noun in a frame of four parts, the place word *ʻi*, the spatial noun, the belonging word *o*, then the thing the position is measured against; in the third the describing verb stands after the name of the thing and says which one is meant.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: the given relationship behind *o*, the four-part frame in its order, and the describing verb after the name of the thing.

questions.prompt: Read *Ona alu lea ʻo le tama.*, *ʻOleʻā alu le teine pē ʻāfai ʻua sau le tama.* and *ʻAiseā na alu ai le tamāloa ʻi le nuʻu?* Which account agrees with the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: In the first, *ona* and *lea* wrap the verb phrase to tell what happened next; in the second, the condition clause follows the main clause, so *pē* stands in front of it; in the third, *ʻaiseā* stands at the front and *ai* after the verb is the pointing-back word.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: the then-construction, the *pē* a following condition takes, and the pointing-back word that goes with *ʻaiseā*.

options.label: B
options.text: In the first, *ona* is the that-word, opening a complement clause that names an event; in the second, the condition clause follows the main clause, so *pē* stands in front of it; in the third, *ʻaiseā* stands at the front and *ai* after the verb is the pointing-back word.
options.explanation: Here *ona* is answered by *lea*, which makes it the then-construction telling what happened next.

options.label: C
options.text: In the first, *ona* and *lea* wrap the verb phrase to tell what happened next; in the second, *pē* opens a reported question, asking whether the boy has come; in the third, *ʻaiseā* stands at the front and *ai* after the verb is the pointing-back word.
options.explanation: No say-verb stands in front of *pē* here, and a condition clause placed after the main clause takes *pē* in front of it.

options.label: D
options.text: In the first, *ona* and *lea* wrap the verb phrase to tell what happened next; in the second, the condition clause follows the main clause, so *pē* stands in front of it; in the third, *ʻaiseā* stands at the front and *ai* after the verb is the who-word, asking who went.
options.explanation: The word *ʻaiseā* already asks why, and *ai* after the verb is the pointing-back word that goes with it.

questions.prompt: What does a belonging-sentence say?

options.label: A
options.text: Where a person or thing is.
options.explanation: That is the where-sentence, which puts a place in the predicate slot instead of an owner.

options.label: B
options.text: Who a thing belongs to.
options.explanation: Correct: the owner stands in the predicate slot with a belonging word in front, and the thing owned follows.

options.label: C
options.text: Who or what somebody is.
options.explanation: That is the naming sentence, which sets two naming parts side by side.

options.label: D
options.text: What somebody did.
options.explanation: That is the verb sentence, which puts an action word after the tense particle.

questions.prompt: Which sentence means "The knife is mine"?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻO laʻu naifi.*
options.explanation: This is the naming part "my knife", which names a thing rather than claiming it.

options.label: B
options.text: *E aʻu le naifi.*
options.explanation: Correct: the belonging form *aʻu* stands as the whole predicate, and a knife is an *a*-word.

options.label: C
options.text: *E oʻu le naifi.*
options.explanation: The form *oʻu* is the *o*-word version of "mine", and a knife takes *a*.

options.label: D
options.text: *E ana le naifi.*
options.explanation: The form *ana* means "his" or "hers", not "mine".

questions.prompt: How do you say "The car is ours" in Samoan?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻO le mātou taʻavale.*
options.explanation: This is the naming part "our car", not a sentence claiming the car is ours.

options.label: B
options.text: *E mātou le taʻavale.*
options.explanation: The belonging word is missing; in this sentence it is required for every owner.

options.label: C
options.text: *E a mātou le taʻavale.*
options.explanation: Correct: the belonging word *a*, then the pronoun *mātou*, then the thing owned.

options.label: D
options.text: *E o mātou le taʻavale.*
options.explanation: This uses the *o* column, and a car is an *a*-word.

questions.prompt: What does *E o le aliʻi le fale* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: The house belongs to the chief.
options.explanation: Correct: the owner *o le aliʻi* is the predicate, and *le fale* is the thing owned.

options.label: B
options.text: The chief is in the house.
options.explanation: That would be a where-sentence, with the place after the tense particle.

options.label: C
options.text: This is the chief's house.
options.explanation: That is the English the fronted shape carries: *ʻO le fale e o le aliʻi.* This sentence has no presenting particle and states whose the house is.

options.label: D
options.text: The chief's house is high.
options.explanation: Nothing here describes the house; *maualuga* would be needed for "high".

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences uses the wrong belonging type for a car?

options.label: A
options.text: *E ana le taʻavale.*
options.explanation: This one is right: a car is an *a*-word, so the *a* column form *ana* fits it.

options.label: B
options.text: *E ona le taʻavale.*
options.explanation: Correct, this is the wrong one: *ona* is the *o*-word form, and a car is an *a*-word.

options.label: C
options.text: *E ana le taʻavale?*
options.explanation: This is the same sentence as a question, "is the car his?", and *ana* is still the right type for a car.

options.label: D
options.text: *E ana le taʻavale ʻeleʻelea.*
options.explanation: This keeps the right type, *ana*, with a describing word added: "the dirty car is his".

questions.prompt: What does the word *tafao* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: wander about
options.explanation: Correct: the word *tafao* is to wander about, and a person who wanders about is a tourist.

options.label: B
options.text: tooth
options.explanation: That is *nifo*, a part of the body; *tafao* names something a person does.

options.label: C
options.text: lean
options.explanation: That is *paʻeʻe*, a describing word for a lean body; the word for "heavy" is *mamafa*.

options.label: D
options.text: big, many
options.explanation: That is *tele*, a describing word for size or number; the word for steel or iron is *uʻamea*.

questions.prompt: In *ʻo le mātou taʻavale* there is no belonging word, and in *E a mātou le taʻavale* there is. Why?

options.label: A
options.text: The belonging word is optional everywhere once the owner is a group.
options.explanation: For a pair or a group it is optional only in front of a naming word; the belonging-sentence prints it for every owner.

options.label: B
options.text: A car has no belonging type, so the word is added for emphasis.
options.explanation: The type comes from the relationship: a car is got and used, so it is an *a*-word, and the sentence has to say so.

options.label: C
options.text: The first is past and the second is present.
options.explanation: The first carries no tense particle at all, and the general particle on the second says nothing about past against present.

options.label: D
options.text: A pair or a group in front of a naming word may leave it out, and a belonging-sentence may not.
options.explanation: Correct: the licence belongs to the naming part alone, so the sentence is where the type has to be decided.

questions.prompt: Which question asks "Whose is the house?"

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻO le ā le fale?*
options.explanation: This asks what the house is: the what-word stands where the who-word should, and there is no belonging form in it.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻO ai e ana le fale?*
options.explanation: The form *ana* is the *a*-word one, and a house is an *o*-word.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻO ai e ona le fale?*
options.explanation: Correct: the who-word leads, and the *o*-word form *ona* answers it later in the sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: *E ona le fale?*
options.explanation: This asks "is the house his?", a yes or no question, not a whose-question.

questions.prompt: In *ʻO le naifi e a le fafine* the thing owned has been pulled to the front. What has to follow it later in the sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: The settled-in-place form *ʻi ai*.
options.explanation: That is what a fronted place requires in a where-sentence, where the place itself moves; here the thing owned moves and requires nothing.

options.label: B
options.text: A second belonging word.
options.explanation: One belonging word is enough, and it stays with the owner where it always stood.

options.label: C
options.text: The presenting particle *ʻo* a second time.
options.explanation: The presenting particle appears once, in front of the thing that moved.

options.label: D
options.text: Nothing; the rest of the sentence stands unchanged.
options.explanation: Correct: the thing moves to the front and leaves no copy behind it.

questions.prompt: A speaker wants to deny that a car is somebody's. What does this chapter say about that?

options.label: A
options.text: Put the not-word *lē* in front of the belonging form.
options.explanation: The chapter gives no such form; the belonging-sentence has no negative.

options.label: B
options.text: Use *lē ʻi ai*, as a where-sentence does.
options.explanation: That form denies a location, not an ownership, and belongs to the where-sentence.

options.label: C
options.text: The belonging-sentence has no negative form, and this book does not cover how ownership is denied.
options.explanation: Correct: this frame is not negated, and the chapter says what is known and stops there.

options.label: D
options.text: Turn it into a question with *ʻO ai*.
options.explanation: A whose-question asks who the owner is; it denies nothing.

questions.prompt: Which account of a describing clause, and of where the one-who word can stand, is right?

options.label: A
options.text: It stands behind a noun with no tense particle of its own; the noun it describes has a job inside it; where no noun is named, the one-who word stands in the noun's place at the front.
options.explanation: Without a tense particle the word behind the noun is a describing verb, as *loloto* is in *le vai loloto*, and not a clause.

options.label: B
options.text: It stands behind a noun and carries a tense particle of its own; the noun it describes has a job inside it; where no noun is named, the one-who word stands in the noun's place at the front.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: the particle is what *le vai e loloto tele* adds, the woman has a job inside the clause of *ʻO le fafine sā alu ʻi le nuʻu*, and *ē* stands at the front where nobody has been named.

options.label: C
options.text: It stands behind a noun and carries a tense particle of its own; the noun it describes has no job inside it; where no noun is named, the one-who word stands in the noun's place at the front.
options.explanation: A clause behind a noun saying what was thought or said is not a describing clause, so the job the noun does inside the clause is part of the definition.

options.label: D
options.text: It stands behind a noun and carries a tense particle of its own; the noun it describes has a job inside it; the one-who word can stand only behind a noun that has been named.
options.explanation: The one-who word also opens the construction where no person has been named, which is what *ʻO lē sā mauʻoloa* and *ʻO ē e mauʻoloa* do.

questions.prompt: What do *mauʻoloa*, *popolevale* and *taufi* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: strong; overanxious; cover
options.explanation: The word for strong is *mālosi*, and the quality word of *ʻO lē sā mauʻoloa* means rich.

options.label: B
options.text: rich; overanxious; want
options.explanation: The word for want is *manaʻo*, and *taufi* is the covering that was done with the liana.

options.label: C
options.text: rich; overanxious; cover
options.explanation: Correct in that order: rich, overanxious, and cover.

options.label: D
options.text: rich; deep; cover
options.explanation: The word for deep is *loloto*, which stands in *le vai loloto*, and the quality word of *ʻO lē sā popolevale* means overanxious.

questions.prompt: In *ʻO le tama e mālosi atu i lo le teine*, which description agrees with the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: The comparison stands outside the describing clause; that is preferred rather than required; the boy's spot inside the clause is left empty.
options.explanation: The whole comparison sits behind the noun it describes, inside the clause, with the than-word phrase keeping its place at the end.

options.label: B
options.text: The comparison stands inside the describing clause; that is required rather than preferred; the boy's spot inside the clause is left empty.
options.explanation: Speakers prefer to build a comparison inside a describing clause rather than state it flat, which is a preference and not a rule.

options.label: C
options.text: The comparison stands inside the describing clause; that is preferred rather than required; the boy's spot inside the clause is held by the pointing-back word.
options.explanation: The boy is the one who is stronger, so his spot stays empty and no pointing-back word stands in it.

options.label: D
options.text: The comparison stands inside the describing clause; that is preferred rather than required; the boy's spot inside the clause is left empty.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: the comparison sits behind the noun it describes, speakers prefer that over the flat statement, and nothing inside the clause stands for the boy.

questions.prompt: What does *le tamāoʻāiga ʻua maua e aʻu uō* mean?

options.label: A
options.text: the wealth my friends got
options.explanation: Correct: the wealth is what was got, nothing inside the clause stands for it, and the agent marker *e* keeps my friends as the ones who did the getting.

options.label: B
options.text: the liana my friends got
options.explanation: The named thing in front is *tamāoʻāiga*, and that word is the wealth.

options.label: C
options.text: my friends who got the wealth
options.explanation: The named thing in front is the wealth, so the phrase describes the wealth and not the friends, as *le meaʻai ʻua maua e le teine* describes the food.

options.label: D
options.text: the wealth that got my friends
options.explanation: The agent marker *e* stands in front of my friends, which makes them the ones doing the getting.

questions.prompt: Which of these gives "The day the girl danced", with an account that agrees with the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻO le aso sā siva le teine.* The time's spot is left empty.
options.explanation: A time leaves a spot that has to be held, and nothing stands in it here.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻO le aso sā siva ai le teine.* The bare *ai* behind the verb is the pointing-back word, and it holds the spot of a place, a time or a cause.
options.explanation: Correct: a time takes the bare pointing-back word behind the verb with no place word in front of it, and a place and a cause take the same shape.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻO le aso sā siva ai le teine.* The word *ai* here is the who-word used in questions.
options.explanation: The Samoan is right and the naming is not: the who-word asks which person is meant and, in the question pattern taught earlier in this book, opens its sentence, while this one points back to the day from behind the verb.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻO le aso sā siva ai le teine.* The bare *ai* behind the verb is the pointing-back word, and it holds the spot of a place or a time but never of a cause.
options.explanation: The Samoan and the naming are both right, and the last part is not: a cause takes the same bare shape as a place and a time.

questions.prompt: In *le fue na taufi aʻi le umu*, what does *fue* mean, and which account of the pointing-back shapes is right?

options.label: A
options.text: Oven; *aʻi* is used only for the thing an action was done with, and bare *ai* is heard in that job too.
options.explanation: The oven word in that phrase is *umu*, and *fue* is the vine itself.

options.label: B
options.text: Liana; *aʻi* is used only for a time, and bare *ai* is heard in that job too.
options.explanation: A time takes the bare shape, as in *ʻO le aso sā oti ai le tamāloa*, and *aʻi* is kept for the thing an action was done with.

options.label: C
options.text: Liana; *aʻi* is used only for the thing an action was done with, and bare *ai* is heard in that job too.
options.explanation: Correct on both: the vine is what *fue* names, and *aʻi* is used for nothing else while *ai* is heard in that job as well.

options.label: D
options.text: Liana; *aʻi* is used only for the thing an action was done with, and no other shape is heard in that job.
options.explanation: The first two parts hold and the third does not, because *ai* is heard for the thing used as well.

questions.prompt: Which account of the goal shape in *ʻO le mea sā alu atu le teine ʻi ai* stays inside the chapter's rule?

options.label: A
options.text: A goal usually takes *ʻi ai* after the verb phrase, and with some verbs, *manaʻo* among them, the clause is heard both ways.
options.explanation: Correct: the pair *ʻi ai* is the usual shape where a movement or a wanting is aimed, and the wanting verb is one of those heard with the place word and without it.

options.label: B
options.text: A goal usually takes the bare *ai* after the verb phrase, and with some verbs, *manaʻo* among them, the clause is heard both ways.
options.explanation: The bare shape is what a place, a time or a cause takes inside the verb phrase, as in *ʻO le nuʻu sā nofo ai le teine*; a goal usually carries the place word in front.

options.label: C
options.text: A goal usually takes *ʻi ai* after the verb phrase, and *manaʻo* takes *ʻi ai* like every other goal verb.
options.explanation: The chapter names *manaʻo* as one of the verbs whose clause is heard both ways, with the place word in front of the pointing-back word and without it.

options.label: D
options.text: A goal usually takes *ʻi ai* after the verb phrase, and every goal verb is heard both ways.
options.explanation: The chapter records that variation for some verbs and names *manaʻo*; it carries nothing that would extend it to every goal verb.

questions.prompt: Three claims: (1) when the named thing is the doer of an action done to something else, the verb must take its long form; (2) a pronoun naming that doer may stand in front of the verb but need not; (3) when the one-who word describes a noun, it matches that noun in number and takes no case marking of its own. Which of them needs correcting?

options.label: A
options.text: None of the three.
options.explanation: Claim 1 does need correcting, because the long form is the shape the verb usually takes and not one it must take.

options.label: B
options.text: Claims 1 and 2.
options.explanation: Claim 1 does need correcting and claim 2 does not: the pronoun may stand in front of the verb, and the clause is complete without it.

options.label: C
options.text: Claims 1 and 3.
options.explanation: Claim 1 does need correcting and claim 3 does not: the one-who word behind a noun matches it in number and takes no case marking of its own.

options.label: D
options.text: Claim 1 only.
options.explanation: Correct: the long form is a preference and not a law, as *fai=a* is in *ʻO tagata sā fai=a le puaʻa*, while claims 2 and 3 state the chapter's rules as they stand.

questions.prompt: Which row gives the one-who shapes correctly: the shape for one particular person and the shape for more than one, what joins in *lē*, and what joins in *e mauʻoloa*?

options.label: A
options.text: *ē* for one particular person and *lē* for more than one; the specific article and the one-who word; the one-who word and the general particle.
options.explanation: The two shapes are the other way round: *lē* is for one particular person, as in *ʻO lē sā mauʻoloa*, and *ē* stands on its own in *ʻO ē e mauʻoloa*.

options.label: B
options.text: *lē* for one particular person and *ē* for more than one; the general particle and the one-who word; the one-who word and the general particle.
options.explanation: The joining in *lē* is the specific article with the one-who word, and the general particle joins the one-who word only in the fused phrase.

options.label: C
options.text: *lē* for one particular person and *ē* for more than one; the specific article and the one-who word; the one-who word and the general particle.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: the number contrast, the article joined to the one-who word in *lē*, and the tense particle run together with it in *e mauʻoloa*.

options.label: D
options.text: *lē* for one particular person and *ē* for more than one; the specific article and the one-who word; the agent marker and the one-who word.
options.explanation: The single *e* of the fused phrase is the general particle of the clause, not the agent marker that stands in front of the one doing an action.

questions.prompt: In *ʻO le tamāloa e manuʻa le vae*, which account gives the meaning of *manuʻa* and both of the chapter's rules about the belonging word?

options.label: A
options.text: Be strong; the belonging word may be left out when the situation makes the relationship plain; a there-is sentence saying somebody has something needs one.
options.explanation: The word for strong is *mālosi*, and the verb of this clause means be hurt.

options.label: B
options.text: Be hurt; the belonging word may be left out when the situation makes the relationship plain; a there-is sentence saying somebody has something needs one.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: the verb is be hurt, the man standing in front makes whose leg it is plain, and the there-is type carries a belonging word naming its owner.

options.label: C
options.text: Be hurt; the belonging word is needed even when the situation makes the relationship plain; a there-is sentence saying somebody has something needs one.
options.explanation: Nothing in this clause says whose leg it is and nothing needs to, because the man is standing in front of it.

options.label: D
options.text: Be hurt; the belonging word may be left out when the situation makes the relationship plain; a there-is sentence saying somebody has something does not need one.
options.explanation: That type is the one place a belonging word is needed: the thing had carries one naming its owner, and the owner is what the clause describes.

questions.prompt: In *Talu ona ʻou sau ʻou te leʻi maua se mea lelei*, which account of the since-word *talu* and the clause after it agrees with the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: It stands behind a word for a stretch of time; the clause after it is opened by no word of its own; that clause usually carries no tense particle.
options.explanation: Two parts are wrong. In this sentence *talu* stands at the head, and it is the pair *talu ai* that stands behind a word for a stretch of time to give "last"; and the clause is opened by the that-word *ona*.

options.label: B
options.text: It stands at the head, in the predicate slot where can and must stand, and marks what follows as the point time is counted from; the clause after it is opened by no word of its own; that clause usually carries no tense particle.
options.explanation: The clause is opened by the that-word *ona*, the same word that opens the clause after can and must.

options.label: C
options.text: It stands at the head, in the predicate slot where can and must stand, and marks what follows as the point time is counted from; the that-word *ona* opens the clause; that clause usually carries no tense particle.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: the predicate slot, the that-word opening the clause, and the empty slot in front of *ʻou sau*.

options.label: D
options.text: It stands at the head, in the predicate slot where can and must stand, and marks what follows as the point time is counted from; the that-word *ona* opens the clause; that clause carries a tense particle of its own.
options.explanation: Nothing stands in the slot in front of *ʻou sau*, because *talu* carries the time for both halves.

questions.prompt: What do *ʻenaʻena*, *vivini* and *faiva* mean, in that order?

options.label: A
options.text: brown; break, of the morning; song
options.explanation: Two meanings are wrong: *vivini* is what a rooster does in *ʻO le vivini a moa, e ʻāmata sāuni ai faiva*, and *faiva* in that same sentence is the fishing trip.

options.label: B
options.text: exhausted; crow, of a rooster; fishing trip
options.explanation: The word *ʻenaʻena* is the colour of the bus in *Ina ʻua malama le taeao, sā sau le pasi ʻenaʻena*: it means brown.

options.label: C
options.text: brown; break, of the morning; fishing trip
options.explanation: The word *vivini* is what a rooster does in *ʻO le vivini a moa, e ʻāmata sāuni ai faiva*: it means crow, of a rooster.

options.label: D
options.text: brown; crow, of a rooster; fishing trip
options.explanation: Correct in that order: brown, crow, of a rooster, and fishing trip.

questions.prompt: Which account of where a since-clause stands, and of what often comes in front of it, agrees with the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: Either order is ordinary and neither changes the meaning; a since-clause often follows a stretch or a point of time named in front of it; where a time is named in front, the counting phrase comes first, then *talu ona* and its clause, then the main clause.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: either order, the "often" of the time expression, and the counting phrase standing first.

options.label: B
options.text: Either order is ordinary but the two differ in meaning; a since-clause often follows a stretch or a point of time named in front of it; where a time is named in front, the counting phrase comes first, then *talu ona* and its clause, then the main clause.
options.explanation: Neither order changes the meaning, which is why the chapter prints the same two clauses both ways, as *Talu ona ʻou sau ʻou te leʻi maua se mea lelei* and *ʻOu te leʻi maua se mea lelei talu ona ʻou sau*.

options.label: C
options.text: Either order is ordinary and neither changes the meaning; a since-clause always follows a stretch or a point of time named in front of it; where a time is named in front, the counting phrase comes first, then *talu ona* and its clause, then the main clause.
options.explanation: A named stretch of time often comes first, as in *ʻO lona tolu o aso talu ona ʻou sau, sā ʻou vaʻai ʻi le teine*, and "often" is where the rule stops.

options.label: D
options.text: Either order is ordinary but the two differ in meaning; a since-clause often follows a stretch or a point of time named in front of it; where a time is named in front, the main clause comes first, then the counting phrase, then *talu ona* and its clause.
options.explanation: Two parts are wrong: neither order changes the meaning, and the counting phrase stands at the front, as in *ʻO lona tolu o aso talu ona ʻou sau, sā ʻou vaʻai ʻi le teine*, where the main clause comes last.

questions.prompt: Which of these gives "last week" (Lit. "in the week since then"), and states both of the things the chapter's Note records about *talu ai*?

options.label: A
options.text: *ʻi le tausaga talu ai*. The pair does the time job alone, and what the pointing-back word points back to inside the pair is not settled.
options.explanation: Two things are wrong: the year is *tausaga*, so that phrase gives last year (Lit. "in the year since then"), and the week is *vaiaso*. The Note also records a second job for the pair, giving the reason for something rather than the time of it.

options.label: B
options.text: *ʻi le vaiaso talu ai*. The pair has a second job, giving the reason for something rather than the time of it, and what the pointing-back word points back to inside the pair is not settled.
options.explanation: Correct: the week phrase gives last week (Lit. "in the week since then"), and the Note records both the second job and the unsettled question of what the pointing-back word reaches.

options.label: C
options.text: *ʻi le vaiaso talu ai*. The pair does the time job alone, and what the pointing-back word points back to inside the pair is not settled.
options.explanation: The Note records a second job for the pair, giving the reason for something rather than the time of it, which this chapter does not teach.

options.label: D
options.text: *ʻi le vaiaso talu ai*. The pair has a second job, giving the reason for something rather than the time of it, and what the pointing-back word points back to inside the pair is the word for the stretch of time.
options.explanation: What the pointing-back word reaches inside the pair is not settled, which is why the chapter says the pair is learned whole.

questions.prompt: In *Ina ʻua sau le teine, sā fiafia le tama* and *Sā māfatia le tama ina ʻua malama le taeao*, which account of a clause opened by the when-word is right?

options.label: A
options.text: It names an event that came after the event of the main clause; the second half of the when-word is the change particle, which is there because the event the clause names was already going on; the clause may open the sentence or follow the main clause.
options.explanation: Two parts are wrong: a clause opened by the when-word names an event that came before the main event or happened together with it, never one that came after it, and the change particle is there because that event is new and turns the situation.

options.label: B
options.text: It names an event that came before the event of the main clause or happened together with it; the second half of the when-word is the change particle, which is there because the event the clause names was already going on; the clause may open the sentence or follow the main clause.
options.explanation: The change particle is there because the event the when-clause names is new and turns the situation the rest of the sentence describes.

options.label: C
options.text: It names an event that came before the event of the main clause or happened together with it; the second half of the when-word is the change particle, which is there because the event the clause names is new and turns the situation; the clause must open the sentence.
options.explanation: The second of the two sentences in the question puts the when-clause after the main clause, and both sides are ordinary.

options.label: D
options.text: It names an event that came before the event of the main clause or happened together with it; the second half of the when-word is the change particle, which is there because the event the clause names is new and turns the situation; the clause may open the sentence or follow the main clause.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: the event stands before the main one or with it, the change particle marks it as new, and either side of the main clause is open to the clause.

questions.prompt: What does *Ina ʻua malama le taeao, sā māfatia le tama* mean, with every Samoan word taken at the meaning this chapter gives it?

options.label: A
options.text: When the morning broke, the boy was exhausted.
options.explanation: Correct on the words: *malama* is the morning breaking, the when-clause names that event, and the main clause says how the boy was left.

options.label: B
options.text: When the morning came, the boy was exhausted.
options.explanation: English can say the morning came for that same event, but the word here is *malama*, the morning breaking; the coming is *sau*, which is what the bus does in *Ina ʻua malama le taeao, sā sau le pasi ʻenaʻena*.

options.label: C
options.text: When the morning broke, the boy talked.
options.explanation: The word *māfatia* is how the boy was left: it means exhausted, and no word in the sentence names talking.

options.label: D
options.text: The morning came when the boy was exhausted.
options.explanation: Two things are wrong. The when-word stands at the head of the clause naming the event the rest is timed against, which here is the clause about the morning; and the word there is *malama*, the morning breaking, not *sau*, the coming.

questions.prompt: In *ʻO le vivini a moa, ʻae ʻāmata le pese*, what does *pese* mean, and which account of a le-phrase set at the head of a sentence is right?

options.label: A
options.text: Fishing trip; the phrase at the head does not name a participant but sets the time the rest of the sentence runs against; one shape puts the main predication on the but-word *ʻae*, and the other is a clause with a tense particle of its own, which never carries the pointing-back word *ai*.
options.explanation: Two parts are wrong. The fishing trip is *faiva*, which stands in *ʻO le vivini a moa, e ʻāmata sāuni ai faiva*, and *pese* is the song; and in that same sentence the clause after the fronted phrase has a tense particle of its own and carries the pointing-back word *ai*, as such a clause usually does.

options.label: B
options.text: Song; the phrase at the head names the participant the rest of the sentence is about; one shape puts the main predication on the but-word *ʻae*, and the other is a clause with a tense particle of its own, which usually carries the pointing-back word *ai*.
options.explanation: Set at the head of everything else, the phrase does not name a participant: it sets the time the rest of the sentence runs against.

options.label: C
options.text: Song; the phrase at the head does not name a participant but sets the time the rest of the sentence runs against; one shape puts the main predication on the but-word *ʻae*, and the other is a clause with a tense particle of its own, which usually carries the pointing-back word *ai*.
options.explanation: Correct on all three: the song, the time the phrase sets without naming a participant, and the two shapes that can follow it.

options.label: D
options.text: Song; the phrase at the head does not name a participant but sets the time the rest of the sentence runs against; one shape puts the main predication on the but-word *ʻae*, and the other is a clause with a tense particle of its own, which never carries the pointing-back word *ai*.
options.explanation: A clause with a tense particle of its own usually carries the pointing-back word, as *ʻO le sau o le pasi, e ʻāmata ai le malaga* does.

questions.prompt: Compare *ʻi le taʻi=tasi aso* with *ʻi taeao o aso taʻi=tasi*. Which account of them is right?

options.label: A
options.text: In the first the time noun heads the noun phrase with the number phrase behind it, and in the second the number phrase heads it with the time noun behind; *taʻi=* goes on the front of a number word, and *tasi* is the word for one; it is not a free-standing word for "every".
options.explanation: The two orders run the other way round: the day phrase puts the number phrase first, and the morning phrase puts the time noun first.
